text:
Performance and Optimization Nightmare "our cs2 experience"
When Counter-Strike 2 was first teased, there were high hopes. The game was supposed to be more "next-gen," with improved graphics, smoother gameplay, and advanced technology that should’ve pushed the franchise into the future. Unfortunately, what we got instead feels like a rushed, undercooked product. Even with a top-tier gaming PC—one that comfortably runs CS:GO at high frame rates—I’m seeing Counter-Strike 2 stutter and lag. It’s as if the game is trying to push something it’s not ready for. FPS drops occur regularly, and the frame rates plummet during high-intensity moments, something that simply wasn’t an issue in its predecessor. The optimization is absolutely terrible.

To make matters worse, there’s an issue with how the game allocates resources. I’ve seen instances where my GPU usage is well below 60%, and my CPU spikes, all while the game stutters to keep up. The result? A frustrating, broken experience where you’re constantly fighting against the game's inherent performance flaws. That might be something you can tolerate in an early beta, but this is the full release, and it's completely inexcusable. It doesn’t matter if you’ve got an RTX 3090 or the latest Intel chip, the game will make you feel like you’re playing on an ancient machine.

Inconsistent Hit Registration and Broken Mechanics
Counter-Strike has always been about precision and skill. A large part of its charm comes from that skill-based combat, where landing shots is directly tied to your aim and timing. But with Counter-Strike 2, the game has broken that core principle.

The so-called “sub-tick” system is a mess. For those who aren’t familiar, this was introduced as a way to improve server tick rates and reduce lag-related issues. Instead of improving things, it has made hit registration feel wildly inconsistent. I’ll be facing an enemy at close range, unload an entire magazine, only to see my shots whiff completely. There’s a delay between the time I pull the trigger and when the shots actually register, and this isn’t just occasional—it’s constant.

You’ll find yourself dying around corners where you’re certain you had the angle, or getting one-tapped by enemies whose bullets seem to bend through walls. It’s not just frustrating, it’s completely maddening. The fundamental mechanics that once made the series great are in shambles. What’s the point of precision aiming when the game itself can’t get the basics right?

Cheating Epidemic: A Competitive Nightmare
One of the most frustrating things about Counter-Strike 2 is the fact that Valve has somehow failed to address the cheating problem in any meaningful way. Aimbots, wallhacks, speed hacks, you name it—cheaters are running rampant in this game, and there’s no real effort to stem the tide.

I’ve spent more time in matches recently reporting players than actually enjoying the game. And even when you do report someone, there’s no guarantee anything will be done about it. Valve’s anti-cheat system feels like a joke, especially when you encounter blatant cheaters who have no fear of being caught. It’s ruining the game’s competitive integrity. What’s the point of trying to be good at a game when your opponents can essentially toggle on god-mode cheats and you’re left helpless?

It’s so bad that I’ve been in matches where cheaters completely dominate, and no one can do anything about it. It destroys the fun of playing competitively. It’s all the more upsetting because Counter-Strike used to be a title where competitive fairness was sacred. Now, it feels like a free-for-all, where cheating is normalized and punished rarely—if at all.

Content Removal: The Soul of Counter-Strike is Gone
One of the biggest slaps in the face to longtime fans is the removal of classic content and game modes. Gone are the beloved modes like Arms Race and Danger Zone, which added variety and fun to the game when you wanted a break from competitive matches. These modes helped flesh out CS:GO, offering something different when the typical 5v5 match just didn’t cut it. Now, with Counter-Strike 2, those modes are mysteriously absent, leaving a void that no amount of new skins or maps can fill.

On top of that, the removal of support for macOS was a baffling decision. Many players in the community, including myself, used to play on Macs, and this sudden exclusion has left a large portion of the fanbase unable to even play the game. For a game that has prided itself on being accessible, this is a huge step back.

Lack of Communication and Developer Inaction
Valve's silence is deafening. The community has voiced its concerns repeatedly, yet the developers have remained almost entirely mute. No clear updates, no explanations for why the game is in the state it’s in—just radio silence. Players are being left in the dark, wondering whether Valve even cares about fixing the game or if they’re just going to move on to the next big title.

This lack of communication has only fueled the anger within the community. We’ve seen them take months to address even the most basic issues, and the fear that Counter-Strike 2 will continue to be neglected is growing every day. The franchise has always had a strong relationship with its fanbase, but that’s rapidly eroding as Valve continues to push out half-baked updates and ignores player feedback.

The State of the Community
Perhaps one of the most disheartening aspects of Counter-Strike 2 is the state of its community. The game has become a toxic wasteland, with constant cheating, connection issues, and poor matchmaking experiences. The player base is frustrated and demoralized, and it shows in how people behave during matches. Once, the competitive nature of CS brought out the best in players, creating an environment of skill and camaraderie. Now, it’s all about getting through the match without tearing your hair out.

The introduction of the new matchmaking system has only made things worse. The rankings feel inconsistent, and there are so many smurf accounts—players intentionally playing at lower levels to dominate newbies—that it’s impossible to climb without running into wall after wall. It’s made the competitive scene feel pointless, with no real progression.

In Conclusion: A Franchise in Decline
After hundreds, maybe thousands of hours spent in the Counter-Strike series, I never thought I’d be here, completely disillusioned and frustrated with the state of the game. Counter-Strike 2 has taken everything that made the franchise great and run it into the ground. What was supposed to be a promising evolution of the series has instead resulted in an unoptimized, broken, and increasingly unpopular title.

It’s hard to recommend the game to anyone anymore. I still have hope that Valve will turn things around, but with each passing update, it feels more like they’re ignoring the core issues that the community is pleading for them to address. Until that happens, Counter-Strike 2 remains an absolute disaster of a release—unplayable, unbalanced, and unrecognizable as the game we all loved.

One major issue with the Counter-Strike series is its lack of a robust anti-cheat system. For instance, games like Valorant and Warzone have background anti-cheat tools that can detect any cheat software running in the background. However, Counter-Strike has so many readily available cheats on the internet that you can easily download one and start playing without any hassle. This is why I am really frustrated playing with a Prime account. I see on social media how these cheats work, and it's really bad sometimes.

I can play Warzone easily and win comfortably, but in Counter-Strike, I encounter all kinds of cheats. These various cheats make the game discouraging, and it's interesting that FACEIT has a really good anti-cheat launcher. But the Counter-Strike team hasn’t implemented an anti-cheat system like FACEIT’s. I love this game, but the cheating issue really gets on my nerves. The reason I've always loved Counter-Strike is its simplicity. It doesn’t have strange equipment and weapons, nor does it have supernatural powers. text:
Counter-Strike 2: A Masterclass in Downgrades

Ah, Counter-Strike 2. The long-awaited, heavily hyped, Source 2-powered evolution of the greatest tactical shooter of all time. And what did we get? A broken mess that makes you appreciate Counter-Strike: Global Offensive—a game we all spent years complaining about.

First, let's talk about the servers. You ever wanted to experience what it’s like to time travel? Well, now you can! Thanks to CS2’s incredible sub-tick system, every gunfight feels like you're guessing where the past version of your opponent might be, while the future version of yourself is already dead. Laggy peeks, input delay, and rubberbanding galore—it’s like Valve found the worst possible way to implement online gameplay and ran with it.

Then, we have the cheaters. Oh boy. If you ever dreamed of playing against professional aimlock enthusiasts in every second game, CS2 has you covered. The VAC system? Think of it as a museum piece—nice to look at but completely useless. Mass reporting doesn’t work, the cheaters never get banned, and somehow, they always win. It's almost impressive.

But don’t worry, CS2 did bring improvements! They gave us volumetric smokes—because that’s what everyone wanted, right? Not better matchmaking, not reliable hit registration, but dynamic, 3D smokes that look cool while you get shot through them by someone using wallhacks.

Meanwhile, Valorant exists, a game that actually runs well, has anti-cheat that does something, and doesn’t make you question if your bullets are real or just imaginary suggestions to the game engine.

Overall, Counter-Strike 2 is like getting a birthday gift from Valve where they take away your old toy and give you a newer, shinier, but completely broken version of it. 0/10 experience when playing, 10/10 experience when uninstalling.

**Counter-Strike 2: A Disheartening Experience with Cheaters and Ineffective Anti-Cheat**

Counter-Strike 2, the highly anticipated successor to the iconic Counter-Strike franchise, brings with it a fresh layer of visuals, mechanics, and updated gameplay. While the core of the game still offers the fast-paced, strategic gameplay fans have loved for years, a major issue continues to plague the experience: cheaters. Unfortunately, this issue has grown rampant, and despite the presence of an anti-cheat system, it remains largely ineffective in providing a fair, competitive environment.

In almost every match, it feels like there's at least one cheater among the players, sometimes more. Whether it's wallhacks, aimbots, or other game-altering exploits, these disruptive players severely degrade the overall experience. What makes it even more frustrating is that the game's anti-cheat system, which was expected to be a solid line of defense, does very little to prevent or mitigate these issues. Instead of feeling like a polished, competitive shooter, the game often feels like a frustrating battle against players who are blatantly cheating and skewing the balance.

Reporting these cheaters doesn’t seem to yield any meaningful results either. The in-game reporting system, which was hoped to deter bad actors, often leaves players feeling powerless. The lack of immediate consequences for cheaters gives the impression that cheating is not being taken seriously by the developers, leading to a negative impact on the game's integrity.

While the gameplay in Counter-Strike 2 has the potential to be fantastic, the overwhelming presence of cheaters and the ineffectiveness of the anti-cheat system create a frustrating environment that severely detracts from the enjoyment. Until more decisive action is taken to address these issues, it’s hard to recommend Counter-Strike 2 to players looking for a fair, competitive shooter experience.

text:
[h1] Intro [/h1]

I've decided to review CS2 due to the incredible amount of spam and jokes I see currently in the review section. I don't think my single review will create a huge impact but in case there's someone out there that's considering playing Counterstrike and looking for some genuine thoughts on the game, I'll tell you about my experience after playing the game for 3 years.

[h1] Counterstrike [/h1]

           At it's core Counterstrike is a sport, I'm not here to argue the legitimacy of Esports so bear with me if you disagree. While it can be played casually, and a lot of people do, this is a game about honing your skills and developing strategies to either defend, or plant a bomb on, a site. And while it's incredibly simple to understand, "just plant the bomb and shoot bro", it's incredibly difficult to master. Up until I began playing Counterstrike, I had never seen a mainstream FPS with such a demand for precision and understanding. Coming from playing Call of Duty on console my entire life, CS was something completely unique and interesting. I love the loop and degrees of difficulty.

[h1] Why Play Counterstrike [/h1]

           Well, mainly because you won't find another game with this type of community and quality gameplay. If you join a casual match, you'll observe that there are people that have been playing for over a decade and sometimes closer to 20 years. That's because CS is historic and continually innovative. It's impossible to summarize CS's immense history so I recommend this video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B35zWsp0r4Y&t=992s . With that context you'll understand that Counterstrike has cemented itself as one of, if not, the best FPS in history. So it might be cool to at least play it once. Especially if you're a Valorant player, you should see where the idea came from. 

[h1] The Ugly [/h1]

             Despite the game itself being innovative and incredibly fun, there are some thing about CS that would make me feel disingenuous if I didn't tell you. Counterstrike has a history of cheaters and creating the most predatory practice in the gaming industry.

[h2] Lootboxes [/h2] 

             Counterstrike invented the lootbox which became insanely lucrative for Valve and prompted the entire mainstream gaming industry to push microtransactions upon us. Thanks Valve! Lootboxes are also a loophole for underage gambling and their existence has resulted in an intricate and complex empire of third-party skin trading/casino websites to take advantage of whoever is unfortunate enough to fall for their schemes. Recently, Coffeezilla made an amazing three part video series covering this entire industry, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q58dLWjRTBE&t=447s 

[h2] Cheating Past [/h2]

             In the past, you'll know if you watch that history video I linked, there's been a couple scandals involving professional CS players/teams cheating. People think this was possible mainly due to Valve's weak anti-cheat. Since those scandals unfolded it's been nearly impossible for pros to cheat, but not out of reach for the everyday person to aimbot in their local CS:GO casual game. Even when I first started playing CS, I was able to observe people obviously cheating and employing bots to get their drops. It was frustrating and confusing how a company with this much money and power could allow this to continue to happen and not take a more aggressive approach to cheating.

[h3] Cheating Present/Community Note [/h3]

               Since CS2 launched and upgrading to Prime Status ($15 to match with other people with the status) I have seen 0, zero, cheaters in Countstrike, premier, casual, etc. But the lasting effects of cheating has left the community battle-scared and paranoid. Too many people look at one lucky shot or someone having a good game and announce to the entire lobby, "wAlLs! tHiS gUy HaS aImBoT!!!!!!" It's honestly pathetic to witness this among so many people playing CS. The lack of accountability or even consideration that someone could best you in a 1v1 or have better game sense is truly embarrassing and is one of the ugliest parts of this community. Another one of the reason I wanted to write this review is because I see so many people reviewing with a single comment summarizing the entire game by saying, "Valve fix anti-cheat" while providing no data, no legitimate proof of cheating occurring. So, potential new player, please don't fall into this victim-hood complex many casual players wear as a crown. 

[h1] Final Thoughts [/h1]

               Despite it's flaws, Counterstrike remains an incredible game that's fun to play regardless of skill level. It's fun to watch pros do their thing at tournaments and your friends clutch a win in casual. There are so many ridiculous and epic moments that have become great memories that I laugh about and celebrate. There are a lot of great people that play that will help you learn and be kind. If you haven't played, and are considering, you're missing out. With that being said, keep an eye out for toxic people: don't be after to block, mute, whatever, it's not worth your time or health. Get Prime Status, this will allow you to access the community of people that have a least showed a little interest in playing. And set a healthy amount of money you're willing to spend on cases a month, if you're into that. Other than that, keep gaming, I hope you win!

Counter-Strike 2 is a great game and, in my opinion, a worthy successor to CS:GO—despite the somewhat strange shooting mechanics. Since the introduction of Subtick, every one-tap feels amazing, but spraying feels incredibly random, which is further amplified by the damage prediction system.

I’ve personally tested the new damage prediction for over 200 hours, and I have mixed feelings about it. On one hand, it feels more responsive; on the other, about a third of the shots result in fake dinks or fake hits. This is especially frustrating when spraying: you see a fake dink, stop shooting because you think you’ve hit the enemy properly, and then end up dying because of it.

That covers the “CS2 vs. CS:GO update” part.

Now, onto the really good aspects: CS2 is an excellent example of a well-designed 5v5 competitive FPS. The core gameplay feels great, and the movement is some of the best I’ve ever seen in an FPS. Meeting new people, playing casual game modes with friends—or even alone—can be really fun! Improving your skills, seeing your progress, and facing increasingly difficult opponents is a rewarding experience.

CS2 perfectly embodies the phrase “easy to learn, hard to master.” Even the best players in the world still have room to improve!

Now, another downside: cheaters. First of all, the situation has improved. But at the same time, it still doesn’t feel truly fixed. Some players are blatantly rage cheating yet remain unbanned. I’ve watched multiple Wingman demos where opponents are locking onto my head—even through walls and smokes—bunny-hopping flawlessly across the map, and wallbanging my teammate and me like crazy. And yet, they’re still not banned. Ridiculous. All we can do is wait for Overwatch to be rolled out to more players.

I could probably go on forever, but I’ll wrap it up here.

All in all: CS2 is a fantastic game that’s fun to play, and it’s great for meeting new people. I would definitely recommend it!
label: positive

text:
As someone who has been a fan of Counter-Strike for years, I had high hopes for CS2. Unfortunately, my excitement quickly turned into frustration as the game has become nearly unplayable due to an overwhelming presence of cheaters. In its current state, CS2 feels like it's more about dodging hackers than enjoying actual gameplay.

It’s almost a given that if you’re queuing, there’s an almost guaranteed chance that you’ll run into someone using some form of cheats—whether it's aimbots, wallhacks, or something even more subtle. This isn’t a problem isolated to just a few games here and there—it’s a constant issue. The game's anti-cheat system, despite being advertised as robust, seems entirely ineffective in handling the sheer volume of cheaters flooding the servers.

This completely breaks the immersion and fun of the game. It's disheartening to be constantly up against players who have an unfair advantage, and it really destroys the competitive integrity that Counter-Strike is known for. You spend more time reporting suspicious players and dealing with frustration than you do enjoying the game itself.

I understand that no game is perfect, and every multiplayer title has some form of cheating, but the current state of CS2 feels like it’s gone from being a competitive shooter to a cheat-infested playground. Until the developers can roll out some effective changes to combat the cheater epidemic, I honestly can’t recommend this game to anyone who wants a fair and enjoyable experience.

Personally haven't had fun in this game yet. Bring back CS:GO

Counter-Strike 2: Now with 200% More Rage and Smokes That Actually Work!

Ah, Counter-Strike 2, the long-awaited sequel to the game that taught us teamwork, patience, and how to creatively insult our teammates in 20 different languages. Valve has finally decided to update CS:GO, and boy, did they bring some changes.

First off, the new smoke physics are so realistic that I’m convinced Valve spent more time simulating grenades than fixing my matchmaking rank. Gone are the days of simple smoke lineups—now every match feels like a science experiment where I accidentally block my own team's vision.

The sub-tick system was introduced to make the game "smoother," but judging by the way I still get headshotted behind walls, I can only assume it’s a new form of psychological warfare. And let’s not forget the movement changes—somehow, jumping feels like I’m playing on ice skates, and bunny-hopping is now an Olympic-level sport.

Graphically, CS2 is gorgeous. The improved lighting and reflections make it easier to admire the scenery while waiting 45 minutes for a match after abandoning a game because my teammate was convinced mid-rush Zeus-only was a good idea.

Overall, CS2 is a fantastic update, full of new mechanics, beautiful visuals, and the same soul-crushing experience of being one-tapped by a guy with 200 ping. 10/10, would uninstall after a losing streak again.

text:
As the successor to CS:GO, CS2 introduces the Source 2 engine, offering improved visuals, enhanced lighting, and a new dynamic smoke system that adds more tactical depth. The official matchmaking servers have been upgraded to 128 tick, improving hit registration and making shooting feel smoother. The game also adopts the MR12 format (12 rounds per half), shortening match durations and aligning with modern esports trends.

CS2 has a massive player base, which has built up a huge market. This means that CS2 isn’t just about traditional FPS gameplay—you can even focus on the skin market. In fact, some have joked that you could use CS2 as a kind of “financial management app.”

Speaking of utility practice, to perform well in CS2 you need to master the callouts for each map and learn how to use your utilities effectively. Unlike mobile games where the trajectory of thrown objects and the landing spot of crosshairs are more predictable, a poorly thrown grenade in CS2 can sometimes accidentally hurt you or your teammates.

However, CS2’s anti-cheat system (VAC) isn’t ideal. Some subtle cheats, like wallhacks, are hard to detect and ban, which contributes to a less-than-optimal environment. Sometimes, even if you’re just unlucky, you might get accused of using cheats.

Counter-Strike 2 (CS2) is the latest installment in the long-running Counter-Strike series, developed by Valve. While it retains the core mechanics that fans love, it introduces several new features and improvements that enhance the overall experience.

Gameplay: The gameplay remains true to the series' roots, with tactical, round-based 5v5 competition. The core formula of terrorists vs. counter-terrorists, with objectives like planting/defusing bombs, remains unchanged. However, CS2 introduces a new Premier ranked mode, which focuses on shorter best-of-24-round matches, increasing the importance of early rounds.

Graphics and Performance: CS2 runs significantly better on modern hardware compared to its predecessor, Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS:GO). The improved graphics and performance make for a smoother and more visually appealing experience.

New Features: One notable addition is the improved buy menu, allowing players to purchase both suppressed and standard M4s. However, some features, like the HE + smoke mechanic, have received mixed feedback from players.

Competitive Play: Competitive play is at the heart of CS2, with the Premier ranked mode taking center stage. Solo and grouped players are placed into teams of five, and matches are intense and fast-paced.

Hacking Issues: Unfortunately, CS2 has been plagued by hacking issues, including wallhacks and aimbots. These hacks allow players to see through walls and automatically aim at opponents, severely disrupting the game's balance and fairness1. Despite efforts to implement an AI-generated anti-cheat system, the problem persists, leading to frustration among players and a decline in the player base.

Conclusion: While CS2 is still in its early stages and has room for improvement, it shows great potential and is a refreshing update to the series. Fans of the franchise will find familiar elements, while new players will appreciate the enhanced performance and new features. However, addressing the hacking issues will be crucial for the game's long-term success.

Overall, Counter-Strike 2 is a solid entry in the series and a must-play for fans of tactical shooters.

Античит Valve, «VAC» (Valve Anti-Cheat), считается многими игроками в CS2 некачественным по следующим причинам:

Медленное обнаружение: VAC может задерживать обнаружение и блокировку читеров, позволяя им играть дольше до наказания.

Ложные срабатывания: В некоторых случаях VAC может блокировать легитимных игроков из-за сторонних программ, что вызывает недовольство.

Медленные обновления: Читы обновляются быстрее, чем сам VAC, что делает систему устаревшей.

Не все читы обнаруживаются: VAC может быть неэффективен против более сложных читов, например, манипулирующих сервером или использующих более скрытные методы.

Зависимость от подписей читов: VAC обнаруживает читы по их подписям, что делает их трудными для идентификации, если читы немного модифицированы.

Эти причины способствуют восприятию того, что античит Valve не справляется с развитием читов.

text:
Unfortunately, it is truly a great game ruined by cheaters.

I had a very long break from CS (and gaming in general), so I was pretty excited to get back and enjoy the gameplay. That happened to be impossible as in at least 20% of your games you'll match up against someone cheating.
Back in 2014-2017 you would also occasionally meet someone cheating, but usually on higher ranks such as LE, LEM, SMFC, GE, that's why (I think) they cheated in the first place — to get to higher ranks and stay there.

Downloading CS years later (and having 0 skill left) I was surprised to find out that now you have silvers and novas flooded with cheaters, which makes 0 sense to me — What is those guys' goal? Why are they ranked so low using cheats? So, in 2025 cheating is not something you occasionally find among high-ranks competing between each other, but rather an issue you simply cannot avoid. Among other things, this makes the game very unfriendly for newbies who expect to play against someone in their skill bracket.

Someone might say "you are just bad and that's why you think others cheat" and while I get this POV, it is simply not the case. I might not be good anymore but I certainly remember the game's physics and stuff like that. It's quite easy to detect a cheater when you played the game for the first time in 2003. (Also, a 0 level, 1 year old, 50 hours in game Steam account having 80% HS% is simply something very, very suspicious).

Also someone might say "just don't play on Valve's servers, go to FACEIT". Firstly, I just want to casully play the game for an hour to relax, not to be all 'competitive' and ruin other's desire to win. Secondly, why can't the game be playable "out of the box" with no need to have any kind of 'add-ons'?

Well, I guess enough for a 'review'. This game will forever stay in my heart as it has brought an incalculable amount of fun into my life back in the days. And it also might bring it to someone today. But unfortunately not to me.

I've played this game since 2016 and i feel that now is the appropriate time to make a review:

I feel like i can speak for the great part of the community when i say that the game has never been in a worst state than today, 


i will go through the main problems this game started showing since the cs2 game launch:


-MAPS: the rework of maps and the overall transition from Source to Source 2 has been painful to say the least, by today standards this is NOT a graphically light game anymore, and the continuous map reworks keep pushing it into that direction, forcing the required hardware cieling higher and inevitably cutting off a part of the player base, if u try to play a premier and for some reason get either Anubis or expecially Train, you are gonna get from 30 to 50% less framerate than in other maps, and the doesnt count particles like smokes or Molotovs.

-SERVERS: the current state of servers as im typing the review 03/02/2025 has been gradually worsening patch by patch. At game launch they announced this new "subticket" system, now im not gonna go into details about what it is because this isnt the point of my review, but at the beiginning it was buggy and unstable to say the least, 3 weeks ago they released a patch that was supposted to fix the problem by changing the way the servers register user inputs, but that ended up making the problem even worst, to the point where having more than 2/3 enemies "interacting" with you means a jitter into the server almost 100% of the times, teleporting you around and usually getting you killed while being behind a wall.
The problem alone shouldnt be that big of a problem but the frequence which this happens is almost astonishing, we're talking from 15 to 20 seconds on a good day and every 5 seconds on a bad day / bad server.

-VAC 3.0: i know this has been a problem since csgo, but i feel that the game became only worst since the cs2 launch, to the point where (by checking vods) you get a cheater every 6 out of 10 games, enemy or teammate.
The situation is in such a bad spot that we have content creators creating entire series about cheaters that they find in games and leaderboards where you can clearly tell which account in the top priemier queue is legit and which isnt.
I understand that this is a hard to fix problem but i thought valve would learn something from their market competitors, i guess they just either pretend that everything is okay or just decide to not really do anything because it would be a huge money investmant that wouldnt really make them profit anything.
This situation is also the result of poorly account sharing policies, where people can buy leveled up accounts for cheap because they usually recive less reports than fresh ones.


(i feel at this point that is necesarry to point out that when speaking about frames and connection, cs is the only game where i have the problems listed above)

Now i will say that i will not stop playing cs, and probably never will (the case gambling has gotten to me way worst than it ever did), but that means that this is a valid excuse the basically slap your community on the face and ignoring every problem that they report.
I just really hope they Fix this game guys, i truly hope so.

Counter-Strike 2 continues the legacy of its predecessors while introducing subtle but impactful improvements that make it stand out. The visuals are crisp, and the game looks great even on mid-tier systems.

CS2 doesn’t really need new content at the moment. What it does, it does well. The sound design is also on point—if you pay attention to the details, you’ll notice how much it adds to the experience, from footsteps to gunshots. It’s immersive, and the audio cues are essential for good gameplay.

Overall, Counter-Strike 2 is a solid entry in the series, maintaining the heart of what made the franchise popular while improving on some key areas. The objective is simple: Terrorists plant bombs, Counter-Terrorists defuse bombs, and you either win or get shot in the head. There are no respawns, so the tension is real. You’ll spend 90% of the round buying the perfect guns, strategizing with your team, and setting up a perfect ambush, only to be one-tapped by someone in the back of the map who’s been camping with an AWP. It's like a symphony of failure and victory, but mostly failure.

Graphics? They Haven't Changed Since 2004... And We’re Okay With That

Let’s be real: The graphics aren’t what they used to be—mainly because they still look like they were made in the early 2000s. But that’s part of the charm! The textures may be a little blurry, but the rush of adrenaline you get when you rush mid on Dust 2 makes up for it. Sure, the walls look like they were painted by a toddler with a crayon, but your ability to dodge grenades isn’t going to change because of that, right?

The People? Rage? Oh, It’s Definitely Coming

Counter-Strike 2 is a game that teaches you about human nature. You’ll meet friendly, tactical geniuses who make callouts like they’re on a military mission. Then, you’ll meet the other 90% of players, who’ll yell at you for your "noob" moves, despite the fact they were probably the ones running into the enemy spawn with a knife. And let’s not even get started on the smurfs (players who are way too good for their rank)—they’re like a special breed of chaos in an already chaotic world.

Weapons? It's All About the "Economy" (and Not in the Fun Way)

Ah, the economy system. You’ve never known true heartbreak until you’ve bought an AWP, been shot in the face with a pistol, and then have to spend the next two rounds with a knife. The guns are all beautifully balanced (except when the guy on the other team has an AWP and you have a Glock), and every match feels like an intense game of "Can We Get Enough Money for the Good Guns?" Spoiler: You probably won’t.

Conclusion:

Counter-Strike 2 is the perfect blend of competitive madness, rage, and fleeting moments of pure joy. You’ll get frustrated, you’ll get sniped, and you’ll probably yell at your screen a lot. But when you win a round with a perfect strategy, it feels like you’ve just solved world peace. That is, until the next round starts and you get killed by someone hiding behind a box with an AK.

Rating: 9/10 – Will make you question your life choices, but also make you come back for more.

As someone who’s have nearly 2000 hours in Counter-Strike 2, I can say this is a fantastic game that brings the intensity, strategy, and skill-based gameplay that the Counter-Strike series has always been known for. The gunplay is incredibly satisfying and responsive, with each weapon feeling distinct and impactful. Whether you're landing a perfect headshot with the AWP or spraying down enemies with the AK, the mechanics are sharp and engaging. The weight and feel of each gun are just *right*, making every match a tense battle that rewards precision, quick thinking, and good team coordination.

The wholesomeness of the game is also something that stands out. There's a sense of community in Counter-Strike 2, with players who genuinely enjoy the competitive nature of the game and appreciate the tactical side of things. The level of teamwork and coordination that’s required to succeed, especially in competitive and Premier modes, makes every match feel like a real team effort. Sure, it can get intense and frustrating at times, but there’s something satisfying about coming together with a good squad to outsmart and outplay the opposing team.

That said, despite all of the positives, there’s one massive issue that severely impacts the experience: 

CHEATING:  Whether you're playing in Premier, Competitive, or Casual lobbies, there’s a huge problem with players using cheats like aimbots, triggerbots, spinbots, wallhacks, radar hacks, bhop script etc. It’s incredibly frustrating when you put in the effort, play well, and then get absolutely steamrolled by a player whose aim is unnaturally perfect or who is spinning around like a maniac with a radar that gives them information they shouldn’t have. The presence of these cheaters ruins the integrity of the game and can really take the fun out of playing.

This is where the game needs improvement, especially in terms of **anti-cheat** measures. While I know Valve has its own system in place, it’s nowhere near as robust as other services like FACEIT, which has a much more effective anti-cheat system. The fact that cheating still runs rampant in Counter-Strike 2—especially in the more competitive modes—really harms the overall experience. While VAC (Valve Anti-Cheat) does catch some cheaters, it feels like it’s not enough to truly stop the cheaters from ruining the game for everyone else. There’s a clear gap that needs to be addressed.

Suggestions for improvement:

1. Stronger Anti-Cheat: The introduction of something similar to FACEIT’s Anti-Cheat system in CS2 could make a huge difference. FACEIT’s system is extremely effective at detecting and banning cheaters in real-time, and its player-driven reports are taken very seriously.

2. Better Detection in Matchmaking: A system that actively monitors suspicious behavior (such as unreasonably perfect aim, unusual movement, or repeated instances of a player being flagged by the community) would help reduce the number of cheaters.

3. Stricter Penalties: Increase penalties for cheating in all game modes, particularly Competitive and Premier. A harsher punishment could be the removal of ranking or harsher bans, as well as faster processing times for reported cheaters.

4. Increased Community Reporting Tools: Allow players to report suspicious behavior more easily, and implement faster response times for investigating reported accounts. Empower the community to help clean up the game.

5. Full Access to System Resources (kernel-level anti-cheat systems): One important suggestion for the devs is to adopt a system similar to Valorant or Apex, where the game has more comprehensive access to the PC’s resources, ensuring that no external software can interfere or improve gameplay unfairly. This would make it significantly harder for players to use third-party programs or cheats to gain an advantage. Allowing the game to better control the hardware and software environment on the player's PC would give it a level of security and fairness that would go a long way in maintaining a clean and competitive environment.

In conclusion, Counter-Strike 2 has the potential to be one of the best multiplayer shooters out there. The gunplay is top-tier, the sense of teamwork is unparalleled, and the game offers a great experience when everything goes right. However, until Valve takes more concrete action against cheaters—especially in the more competitive settings—it will continue to be held back by this issue. For the game to reach its full potential, stronger anti-cheat measures and more control over the player's system are a must. Let’s hope the devs are listening!

[h3][b]Counter-Strike 2 – A Legendary Shooter With a Fading Legacy[/b][/h3]

As someone who has been playing Counter-Strike since its early days as a Half-Life mod in 1999, Counter-Strike 2 should have been an exciting new chapter for the series. And in some ways, it is. The improved Source 2 engine brings updated graphics, smoother movement, and better responsiveness. The smoke grenade physics are a game-changer, adding new layers of strategy. At its core, CS2 still delivers the same tight, skill-based gameplay that made the franchise legendary.

But, despite these improvements, the biggest issue that has plagued Counter-Strike for years remains—cheaters. And unfortunately, it's only getting worse.

[h3][b]The Good: A Fresh Coat of Paint on a Classic Formula[/b][/h3]

Valve’s improvements to the game’s engine have made CS2 look and feel modern while keeping the classic gameplay intact. Gunplay is as crisp as ever, movement feels smoother, and the revamped maps bring a fresh visual appeal. The sub-tick system, while controversial, aims to reduce inconsistencies in hit registration, and when everything works as intended, the game feels great.

[h3][b]The Bad: The Cheater Problem is Worse Than Ever[/b][/h3]

But no matter how polished the mechanics are, none of it matters when cheaters run rampant in nearly every match. From wallhacks to aimbots, CS2 has become an increasingly frustrating experience for legitimate players. Valve's anti-cheat system, VAC, simply isn’t doing enough to keep up with the problem. The rise of spin-botters, rage cheaters, and even blatant hackers in ranked games makes it incredibly difficult to enjoy Counter-Strike the way it was meant to be played.

For veteran players like me, who have spent decades mastering the mechanics, positioning, and game sense, it's heartbreaking to see skill take a backseat to those willing to exploit the system. Gone are the days of tense, skill-based firefights—too often, matches are ruined by cheaters who erase any sense of competition.

[h3][b]A Community Divided[/b][/h3]

The Counter-Strike community is one of the most passionate in gaming, but frustration is growing. Many longtime players have walked away due to the overwhelming presence of cheaters, while others remain hopeful that Valve will finally take meaningful action. But with each passing year, it gets harder to believe that a real solution will come.

[h3][b]Final Verdict: A Love-Hate Relationship[/b][/h3]

Counter-Strike 2 should be the ultimate evolution of a legendary franchise, but its biggest flaw remains unaddressed. The refined gameplay, graphical upgrades, and new mechanics are overshadowed by a cheating epidemic that makes ranked play feel like a waste of time. For casual play or private matches with friends, it can still be a great experience. But if you’re looking for fair, high-level competition, CS2 is becoming increasingly difficult to enjoy.

text:
I am completely new to the Counter-Strike franchise, with my first experience being with the release of CS2. I honestly steered clear of the game because of all of the negative things you hear about it. However, having played basically every competitive FPS game, including Apex Legends, R6S, OW, Valorant, and many more, I have to say, CS2 has by far the best gun play out of any competitive FPS game, and it's not even close. Games like Valorant, which is a direct competitor, just doesn't nail it. Everything is so slow and small in Valorant that aiming well isn't really a necessity. Your aim is never challenged because the game is slow paced and more focused on gimmick abilities. Comparing it to CS2 is like night and day. 

There is also so much depth to shooting in CS2. You don't have to stand completely still like in Valorant, you can do slight movements, crouches and adjustments that completely change the engagement. It challenges your enemies aim, as they no longer have to click a stationary target. That doesn't mean jitter-strafing like in Overwatch is an issue though, thanks to the acceleration mechanic of movement in CS2.

I think what makes CS2 gun play so addicting is how central to the gameplay loop the gun play really is. Unlike Valorant, Overwatch, or Apex, where the main thing that shifts an engagement is your ability usage, in CS2 you rely almost completely on outplaying your opponent with raw mechanics. There are of course utility, but they are nowhere as pivotal as in Overwatch, where the game is essentially decided by whichever team is trading their ultimate abilities better.

All in all, I'm happily surprised by how fun and addicting CS2 gun play is. However, I have been playing on 0-2ms of ping. Having heard ping makes a huge difference in CS2, I cannot say if the gun play would feel as solid on 30+ ping. There is also a huge issue with cheating in competitive and premiere gamemodes, as VAC unfortunately isn't as good at catching cheaters as their competitors anti-cheats like Vanguard and Easy Anti-Cheat. If you end up taking the game seriously and want to improve to the top ranks, playing on Faceit is a necessity. Premiere is unplayable even in 10-15k range.

text:
Counter-Strike 2: The Game That Makes You Question Your Life Choices, But You’ll Be Back Anyway

Look, Counter-Strike is not for everyone. In fact, if you’ve ever played it, you’ve probably had that moment where you stop and wonder: What am I doing with my life? Why am I putting myself through this cycle of frustration, rage, and occasional victory? But then, CS2 happens. Maybe you get a clutch round. Maybe you finally top the leaderboard. But, let’s be honest most of the time, the game ends with you screaming at the screen, wondering why you keep putting your mental health on the line for the sake of virtual victory.

But here's the kicker no matter how many times you ask yourself if it’s all worth it, we all end up coming right back a few months later, dipping our toes into the salt ridden toxicity that is CSGO I mean, CS2 (same thing, right?). It's like a bad relationship that you know will let you down, but you keep returning anyway, thinking, “This time will be different.”

As a South African, I can tell you that the things said in the lobbies especially in voice chat would probably get us all thrown in jail or at the very least placed on some kind of government watchlist. Seriously, if anyone overheard some of the conversations happening in those lobbies, there would be an immediate investigation. It’s basically the verbal equivalent of opening a can of red-hot chili flakes and tossing them into the air, just to see how much chaos it can cause. Yet, in a strange way, it’s the one place we all gather to release our pent up toxicity, because who needs therapy when you’ve got a ragtag group of 12-year olds calling you every name under the sun while you’re trying to defuse a bomb?

In conclusion, CS2 is like a chaotic, toxic rollercoaster that will make you want to uninstall it every 10 minutes, but you’ll always find yourself back on that ride a few months later, laughing, crying, and wondering how the heck you survived the last match. Would I recommend it? Absolutely. Would I recommend it to anyone I like? Well, that's a different story.

Vulkan and DirectX API support for enhanced performance.
Improved anti-cheat measures via VAC.
Steam integration for inventory and matchmaking.
Some limitations include the absence of robust modding tools and community servers compared to earlier versions. Optimization issues may occur on older systems, but the game performs well overall.

text:
Counter-Strike 2  marks a significant leap forward in the Counter-Strike franchise, combining its iconic gameplay with modernized features. As a long-time player, I’ve thoroughly enjoyed my time with the game, but it does come with its fair share of ups and downs.

Pros:

Improved Graphics: CS2 runs on the Source 2 engine, bringing stunning visual enhancements. Maps like Dust2 and Mirage are beautifully reworked with improved lighting and textures, making them feel fresh without losing their identity.
Responsive Gameplay: The updated tick rate system ensures smoother and more consistent gameplay. This change, especially for competitive players, eliminates the frustration of missed shots due to server limitations.
Dynamic Smokes: The rework of smoke grenades adds a new tactical depth. Smokes now interact with the environment dynamically, dispersing around objects and even being temporarily dissipated by grenades.
Free Upgrade: For CS:GO players, CS2 is a free upgrade, allowing veterans to transition without additional cost.
Sound Improvements: Directional audio is more refined, aiding situational awareness. Footsteps and gunfire are clearer, making the sound design a core part of the strategy.

Cons:

Performance Issues: Despite the visual improvements, the game can be resource-heavy. Many players with mid-range PCs report frame rate drops and stuttering.
Matchmaking System: While there are efforts to improve matchmaking, issues like uneven teams and occasional smurfing persist, which can be frustrating in ranked play.
Limited Content at Launch: Some maps and modes from CS:GO are missing in CS2, leaving long-time players yearning for their return.
Learning Curve: The new features, while exciting, come with a learning curve. Players need time to adapt to the updated mechanics, especially in competitive settings.
Cheating Concerns: Like its predecessor, CS2 struggles with cheaters. Although anti-cheat measures have improved, they are not foolproof.

Overall Impression:

Counter-Strike 2 successfully modernizes the classic experience while retaining its core competitive spirit. It’s a must-play for fans of the series, but new players and veterans alike should be prepared for some growing pains. With time, updates, and community feedback, CS2 has the potential to become one of the best entries in the franchise.

Rating: 8/10

Counter-Strike 2 Review: A Frustrating Experience with Cheats and Stagnation

As a long-time fan of the Counter-Strike franchise, I was excited to dive into Counter-Strike 2 (CS2) with high hopes for a fresh and balanced gameplay experience. However, after considerable hours invested in the game since its release, I find myself increasingly disappointed and frustrated with its current state.

First and foremost, the rampant cheating in CS2 has taken away from the core gameplay experience. It’s disheartening to see well-known cheating tools and aimbots flooding the servers, making matches feel less about skill and more about who can exploit the game better. The lack of effective anti-cheat measures has led to a scenario where many players, including myself, are often left questioning whether our defeats are a result of genuine skill discrepancies or the presence of cheaters. This is especially disheartening given the competitive nature of the game, where every match should feel earned and legitimate. 

Moreover, I was hoping that CS2 would see regular updates that would enhance gameplay and address community feedback. Unfortunately, the updates have been sparse and lack the depth and impact that we desperately need. Whether it's tweaking weapon balance, fixing bugs, or introducing new content, the lack of meaningful updates has created a stagnant environment that fails to keep players engaged or excited about the game. It feels like Valve is stuck in a holding pattern, and the community is left with the same old grievances.

It’s also worth mentioning that the progression and reward systems could use a serious overhaul. Compared to its predecessors, the current system feels unnecessarily grindy, and without significant gameplay changes or invigorating new modes, the motivation to keep grinding diminishes.

In conclusion, while CS2 has the potential to be a phenomenal entry in the Counter-Strike series, the overwhelming presence of cheats and the lack of substantial updates have marred the experience for many players, including myself. I truly hope that Valve can address these issues and reignite the community's passion for the game, but as it stands, CS2 is a reminder of what could have been rather than a shining emblem of improvement. Here’s to hoping for change in the near future.

text:
Today it's been exactly 25 years when I started playing Counterstrike Beta 5.2 at January 10, 2000 with some friends, spending up to 300 DM (German "Mark") every month paying for the internet traffic without available flatrates in Germany. 

Time jump: Last week, I joined my 12-year-old son in a Fortnite match while he was playing with his friends. The map was kinda Deathmatch-Mode. I don't know much about Fortnite. But the kids were impressed about the shooter skills of such "an old man" like me. So I showed them the game I learned how to play competitive shooters in my early 20s: Counterstrike. 

After installing CS2 it was me being impressed. For a long time I avoided shooter games, because I got older and slower and found other games I liked more. But CS2... wow... it's technically a masterpiece. The tick rate, the maps, the physics, the graphics, the unbelievable responsive aiming, gunplay and feedback. A few matches and the feeling and the "just one more match"-fever caught me again.

But: I am older. I am slower. And first hours back in CS after more than 20 years felt like hell. Surviving more than 10 seconds every round was my first challenge I had to master. It took me 10 hours playtime until I managed to win my first duel again. But for me, this felt like winning an e-sports tournament. Another 10 hours later my kill/death-rate raised from 1:10 to 1:2, and at this level it's fun to me again. Hey, I am almost 50 years old, and didn't play competitive shooters for many years. I will never become a top player or maybe even a good player again - but meanwhile I'm not completely useless for my team. For me, that's fun enough.

Sometimes I wish the community would be less toxic. Some things never changed in 25 years. A lot of players still cann't handle their personal frustration and stress level: "Noob team!", rage quit and flaming in voice chat are still present. In my first casual matches I sometimes got rage-vote-kicked by my team for my bad performance in placing or defusing the bomb. 

On the other hand, there are team mates which helped me a lot to get better again by giving hints, explanations and offering help. 

So, long story, but what I wanted to tell you: If you manage to keep your motivation up during the hardest first hours you will ever have in a computer game, you will finally get access to the best competitive shooter in the world. Learn to play Counterstrike and other shooters feel like throwing cans at a festival. The bigger the challenge, the more rewarding feeling is granted.

See you on de_dust!

text:
[h1]Counter-Strike 2 Review: The Game, Skins, and the Industry's Shadows [/h1]

Counter-Strike 2 (CS2) represents Valve’s ambitious leap to redefine its iconic FPS for modern times. It’s smoother, more visually appealing, and has the backbone of Source 2 to enhance mechanics and bring new life to the competitive gaming scene. However, beneath the polished exterior lies a game entangled in the nuances of its most defining feature—skins—and some longstanding systemic challenges.

 [h2]CS Skins: The Original NFTs [/h2]
Before CS2's release, there was always the looming question of longevity. Could this be the game’s last iteration? Would the digital inventory of expensive skins persist into the future? CS2 answered this decisively: skins are here to stay.

Counter-Strike skins are often hailed as the original NFTs, setting a benchmark long before the term took the world by storm. These cosmetic items hold tangible value, functioning as both collector’s items and pseudo-currencies. Unlike traditional assets, inflation, economic downturns, and market volatility don’t impact CS skins in conventional ways. This is why they remain a unique store of value.

The permanence of these skins in CS2 reinforces their role in gaming culture and investment portfolios alike. As more players hold onto their virtual collections—fewer cashing out for physical luxuries like Steam Decks or PC upgrades—the scarcity grows, further bolstering their value. The economy now seems indomitable; that is, until you consider the systemic risks.

 [h2]The Gambling Shadow [/h2]
One of the darkest corners of Counter-Strike’s skin economy lies in gambling. Since the early days, third-party websites have allowed players to wager their skins on games of chance, often engaging underage audiences in these activities.

CS2 has only exacerbated this issue with its renewed focus on skins. For children or teenagers who may not fully comprehend gambling risks, skin casinos and loot box-style systems prey on impulsivity. The fact that Valve, through CS2, has not clamped down on third-party skin betting perpetuates a hazardous ecosystem where some of the most vulnerable players are at risk of addiction and financial exploitation.

Despite public outcry over the years, gambling connected to CS skins remains as pervasive as ever. It's an ethical dilemma: how can Valve leverage an immensely profitable skin economy while addressing its exploitative underbelly? So far, there seems to be no clear answer.

 [h2]No Budget to Counter Cheaters [/h2]
Counter-Strike’s reputation has always been marred by cheaters, and CS2 is no exception. While Valve promised VAC Live and improved anti-cheat measures with CS2, cheating remains rampant.

What frustrates the community most isn’t just the existence of cheats but the perception that Valve lacks the budget or willingness to address the issue comprehensively. Given the billions made from skin trades, players rightfully ask: why isn’t a portion of this revenue reinvested into maintaining competitive integrity?

Cheaters not only degrade the experience but drive players away. While CS2's mechanics are tight, and its design is revolutionary, the lack of robust anti-cheat measures overshadows these advancements. At the core of any multiplayer game is fairness, and without stronger efforts in this area, CS2 risks alienating its community over time.

 [h2]The Skins Economy as a Lifeboat and a Risk [/h2]
The only significant risks to CS skins used to be fears of the game dying or Valve launching a new installment that wouldn’t carry over inventories. With these risks mitigated by CS2, the skins economy is stronger than ever, becoming a cultural and economic phenomenon. However, this shift also has broader implications.

Unhealthy Speculation: The value of skins increasingly resembles speculative investment markets. Players hoard rare skins not for gameplay but as financial hedges, encouraging behavior akin to stockbroking rather than gaming.
Limited Accessibility: With top-tier skins priced in the tens of thousands of dollars, much of CS2’s skin content is unattainable for casual or younger players. Instead of unifying the player base, this economic stratification exacerbates divides between the elite investors and everyday gamers.
Conclusion: A Beautiful, Flawed Giant
Counter-Strike 2 refines and enhances a beloved gaming formula, solidifying its status as a dominant force in esports and gaming culture. The evolution of skins, from in-game cosmetics to bona fide assets, has elevated the franchise into uncharted territory where gaming meets economic theory.

Yet, beneath its glittering surface lies a murky world of unchecked gambling and systemic issues like cheating that betray the core experience. Until these shadows are addressed, CS2 will remain a flawed masterpiece—equal parts exhilarating and ethically complicated.

For Valve, CS2 represents an extraordinary opportunity but also a solemn responsibility: to ensure that this powerhouse of a game doesn’t overshadow the very players who make it legendary.

Counter-Strike 2 Review: A Return to Classic Gameplay… with a Major Anti-Cheat Problem

Counter-Strike 2 has finally made its way into the gaming scene, bringing with it the promise of refined graphics, modernized mechanics, and a new coat of paint on the classic formula that made its predecessors so beloved. The legacy of Counter-Strike is rich, and it holds a special place in the hearts of FPS enthusiasts worldwide. So, when Valve announced Counter-Strike 2, expectations were understandably high. And while the game delivers in some areas, one massive, glaring issue continues to plague the experience—its anti-cheat system, or rather, the lack of an effective one. But let's take a deeper dive into the game as a whole, with an emphasis on this frustrating problem.

Gameplay & Visuals: A Solid Foundation
At its core, Counter-Strike 2 does what it does best—it offers fast-paced, skill-based FPS action with a focus on strategy and team coordination. The gunplay feels incredibly satisfying, with each weapon maintaining its signature feel from previous iterations of the series. The tweaks made to weapon handling and recoil are subtle but effective, improving both the new-player experience and the satisfaction of veteran players who know the ins and outs of every firearm.

The visuals are also noticeably improved. The Source engine has been overhauled, and while it retains the familiar look of its predecessors, there’s a noticeable upgrade in textures, lighting, and overall environmental detail. Maps look more vibrant and alive, while the iconic locales like Dust2 and Mirage retain their core design while benefiting from new visual enhancements. There’s a sharpness and polish that’s been brought to the game that feels modern, even if it’s not quite on par with some of the graphical standards set by other AAA shooters in the market today.

However, as beautiful as the game looks, all of this is marred by one insufferable flaw—the anti-cheat.

The Anti-Cheat Problem: A Game-Changer in the Worst Way
Let’s get straight to the point: Counter-Strike 2’s anti-cheat is an absolute disaster. This is, by far, the most frustrating aspect of the game, and it drags down the overall experience to the point where it’s hard to recommend the game in its current state.

Since the game’s launch, it has been plagued by cheaters and hackers, many of whom are able to exploit a system that simply doesn’t seem to be up to the task of handling the sheer volume and variety of cheating techniques out there. The community has been vocal about the problem, and rightfully so. It’s one thing to have a few isolated incidents of cheating in any multiplayer game, but in Counter-Strike 2, cheating feels like a constant presence.

Even with Valve’s recent attempts at improving the situation, including tweaks to their anti-cheat software and the introduction of new detection mechanisms, the problem persists. It’s almost as if Valve is stuck in a vicious cycle of trying to patch things up without addressing the root of the issue. The result? Countless players logging in only to be immediately confronted by a blatant wallhack or aimbot user, or worse, experiencing gameplay sessions where the outcome is already decided by the presence of cheaters.

The worst part is the inconsistent enforcement. Overwatch, the community-driven system in place to help identify and punish cheaters, seems to be working less effectively than ever before. The community is left wondering if any real action is being taken, as cheaters are frequently able to fly under the radar, ruining the experience for others. It feels like Valve is more focused on ensuring that the game is visually appealing and polished, while leaving the backbone—the anti-cheat—weak and vulnerable.

This isn’t just an inconvenience for casual players or those looking for a fair match. It’s a game-breaking issue for competitive players, especially those who take the game seriously. For players who put time and effort into mastering the mechanics, climbing the ranks, and refining their skills, the constant threat of cheaters erases any sense of accomplishment or fairness. When you lose a match because someone is walling or using an aimbot, it doesn’t matter how good you are—it feels like the game is rigged against you.

The Community’s Frustration: A Toxic Environment
As you might expect, the ongoing issues with anti-cheat have bred an increasingly toxic atmosphere in the Counter-Strike 2 community. With so many players frustrated by the lack of proper enforcement, it’s easy for bitterness and anger to seep into the player base. There’s a growing sense of distrust—many players are questioning the legitimacy of ranked matches and wondering if they’ll ever get a fair shot at winning.

Moreover, the perception of a game overrun by cheaters often leads to players abandoning games early, or worse, throwing matches. This not only degrades the quality of each match but also discourages newer players from sticking around, as they realize that, despite their best efforts, they’re up against a system that doesn’t seem to care. For new players looking to dive into the competitive scene, the anti-cheat problem could be enough to drive them away entirely.

The issue is compounded by Valve’s apparent lack of transparency. There’s been little communication from the developers on how they plan to solve this issue, and it’s left the community grasping at straws. We need clearer, more consistent communication on what’s being done to address the anti-cheat system. Is Valve working on new measures? Are they planning on rolling out significant improvements? The silence is deafening, and it only fuels more frustration.

The Impact on Long-Term Playability
One of the things that made Counter-Strike 1.6 and Counter-Strike: Global Offensive so enduring was the ability to jump into a match with the confidence that, no matter how hard you fought, your skills and teamwork would be the deciding factor. Sure, there were always the occasional cheaters, but they were rare enough that they didn’t ruin the experience. The Counter-Strike 2 anti-cheat problem changes that.

The longevity of the game now seems uncertain. A game that prides itself on its competitive nature is held back by a system that fails to protect players from unfair advantage. And as any experienced player knows, if you can’t trust the competitive integrity of a game, then there’s little reason to stick around.

Conclusion: A Game Full of Potential, But in Dire Need of Attention
Counter-Strike 2 has all the pieces of what could be an incredible FPS experience—tight gameplay, gorgeous visuals, and a legacy that few other games can match. Unfortunately, these strengths are overshadowed by an anti-cheat system that feels outdated, ineffective, and downright frustrating. Until Valve can get this issue under control, Counter-Strike 2 will remain a game plagued by the same old problems that have persisted in the series for years.

It’s clear that Valve needs to dedicate more resources and attention to improving their anti-cheat technology. If they don’t, Counter-Strike 2 risks becoming yet another FPS that’s held back by its inability to create a fair and competitive environment for players. Whether you’re a newcomer or a seasoned veteran, don’t expect to have a smooth, uninterrupted experience just yet. For now, the game is more about enduring the anti-cheat problems than enjoying the competitive action. Until Valve steps up their game, Counter-Strike 2 is a hard title to recommend to anyone looking for a truly fair online shooter experience.

If Valve ever decides to fix this issue—and we sincerely hope they do—Counter-Strike 2 could easily become the competitive shooter to beat. Until then, however, you’ll likely find yourself constantly checking for cheaters, and that’s a major disappointment.

Counter-Strike 2: My Honest Experience – The Good, The Bad, and The Frustrating

As someone who’s been playing Counter-Strike for years, the transition to Counter-Strike 2 was both exciting and nerve-wracking. When it dropped, I was ready to embrace the new era, and while there are things I absolutely love about the game, there are definitely parts that left me shaking my head. Here’s my experience, the good and the bad.

The Good: Why CS2 Feels Fresh
Visuals That Pop
The first thing that hit me was how gorgeous the game looks. Maps like Inferno and Overpass feel alive now. The lighting, textures, and revamped physics make everything feel more immersive. Even smoke grenades have been reimagined—watching smokes interact with gunfire and explosions is so satisfying. It’s a small detail, but it adds a tactical layer that wasn’t there before.

Skins and Floats Are Next-Level
I’ve always been a bit of a skin collector, and in CS2, they’ve really stepped up. My M9 Bayonet Doppler looks like a work of art with the updated reflections. The way floats affect how skins look is so much more noticeable now. Seeing a 0.00 float glisten or a battle-scarred AK47 actually feel like it’s been through a war adds a level of personality to my inventory. As a trader, this just adds more excitement to finding the perfect skin.

Gameplay Feels Smoother
One thing I’ve noticed is how much better movement and shooting feel. It’s hard to explain, but the new tick-rate system makes every shot feel precise. The game is more responsive, which makes clutch moments even more intense. The updated audio also helps—I can actually tell where footsteps are coming from now, which is a game-changer.

The Bad: Why CS2 Sometimes Makes Me Want to Rage Quit
The Cheater Problem is Still Here
This is the biggest issue for me. It’s so frustrating to queue up for a matchmaking game only to run into someone blatantly walling or aim-hacking. The VAC system is still way too weak. Sure, it might catch the occasional cheater, but not nearly enough to stop them from ruining games. It feels like every other match has at least one suspicious player, and honestly, it’s exhausting.

Matchmaking Issues
Speaking of matchmaking, it’s a mess. I’ve had games where my team is full of silvers while the enemy team seems stacked with global elites. It’s impossible to play properly when the skill levels are this inconsistent. And don’t even get me started on the long queue times—I’ve waited almost ten minutes just to get thrown into an unbalanced game. It’s a letdown, especially when all I want is a competitive and fair match.

Hard for Newcomers, Brutal for Casuals
I’ve tried convincing a few friends to get into CS2, but they’ve been turned off by how unforgiving it is. Without proper tutorials or training options, new players are thrown straight into the deep end. Even as a seasoned player, I’ve had my share of rough games, so I can only imagine how frustrating it must be for someone just starting out.

Final Thoughts: A Mixed Bag
Counter-Strike 2 is a beautiful game with tons of potential. The updated visuals, refined gameplay, and enhanced skins make it feel like a true next-gen experience. But at the same time, the cheater problem and matchmaking issues really drag it down. It’s hard to fully enjoy the game when I’m constantly worrying about whether my next match will be ruined by a hacker.

For me, it’s still worth playing—I’ve had some incredible moments and clutches that remind me why I love Counter-Strike. But if Valve doesn’t step up with a stronger anti-cheat system and fix matchmaking, I can see this game losing players over time. It’s frustrating because CS2 has the potential to be the best version of Counter-Strike yet.

Final Verdict: 7/10
It’s a love-hate relationship. When it’s good, it’s great. But when it’s bad, it’s maddening.

Counter-Strike 2: A Love Letter to Chaos, Bullets, and Questionable Life Choices

Ah, Counter-Strike 2—the game where you either emerge victorious like an Esports god or question every decision that led you to boot it up. It’s fast-paced, brutally unforgiving, and somehow still manages to be the most fun you’ll have while simultaneously contemplating uninstalling it every other round.

The Good:
The new Source 2 engine was chef's kiss a much-needed face-lift. Graphically, it finally looks like a game from this decade rather than a relic you’d find on a dusty LAN party hard drive. Landing a kill feels incredibly rewarding—your palms sweat, your heart races, and for a brief moment, you’re convinced you’re the main character.

The Bad:
CS:GO was a polished diamond; CS2 feels more like a shiny rock someone handed you and said, “Close enough, right?” Desync issues on servers with even slightly questionable ping will have you shooting ghosts and yelling at your screen like it owes you rent. And let’s not forget the absolute lack of new operations—Valve, buddy, are you okay? You’ve got time for new cases but not fresh content? Is Cache being held hostage somewhere? Blink twice if you need help.

The Ugly:
Cheaters. Oh boy, the cheaters. Every match feels like a lottery: will you get a regular player, or will you face someone who’s clearly starring in Wallhacks: The Musical? Valve needs to stop giving us shiny skins and focus on building an anti-cheat system that doesn’t feel like it’s being run on Windows 98.

Final Thoughts:
Despite all its quirks, frustrations, and moments where your SMG magically transforms into a laser beam mid-sprint, Counter-Strike 2 is undeniably fun. It’s easy to pick up, painfully hard to master, and rewarding in a way that keeps you coming back for more punishment. If you enjoy tactical gameplay, adrenaline-fueled firefights, and the occasional existential crisis, Counter-Strike 2 is your game.

Would I recommend it? Absolutely—to anyone who truly hates themselves but loves a good headshot highlight reel. 9/10, will queue again... reluctantly

text:
I would honestly love to recommend CS2 as it can be a very fun FPS and has a much higher skill-ceiling than most FPS games nowadays. However, in the state its in at the moment, I just can't seriously recommend it to people. Here's why:

I've never played too much of Counterstrike, back when it was CS:GO, and where most of my hours have come from, I would hop on with friends from time to time and play some ranked to see how far I'd get but it wasn't really a regular thing for me. I sucked pretty badly at it to be honest but it was just fun to play with mates (they have considerable more hours and skill at this game) when we were all available so I didn't really mind it. We had some fun times on it, playing ranked, doing private server mini-games and such and then we sort of stopped playing it for one reason or another.

Then CS2 came out, and I saw my friends playing it again so I decided to give it a go as well. Coming back to the game after so long felt really strange but the visuals had definitely been improved! And the smokes/molotov effects looked amazing. My friends had already started playing ranked and FACEIT (for those that know) so I figured I'd give it a go too. Hereby Introducing "Premier mode". Premier mode is one of CS2's ranked modes. Its the classic 5v5 Terrorists Vs Counter Terrorists. You begin the lobby by banning maps between the 2 teams and then you choose a side to play, then finally the match starts. So I decided to play a couple on my own to get my rank since everyone starts without one and you need to win 10 games to reveal it. I won 3 matches the first night I tried and after the 3rd win I got a notification saying that only a maximum of 2 wins a day will count towards revealing your rank. But......why?. I understand that maybe this is to stop bot accounts/cheaters to try and join in since they don't need to pay for the game, but I had played the game in the past, and my account isn't new. It just didn't make sense. Anyways a bit of persistence and some eye-rolling later and finally I got the 10th win!! I can finally play with my mates :D, or well with their smurfs for now since I was too low rating to play with their main accounts. And now beginneth the story of a whole different problem....

Cheaters.

This game is full of them. Usually I see reviews of people complaining about this and think "yeah aight whatever" but honest to god after playing the game It makes me want to create a review and say the same thing. I've never had this bad of an experience with cheaters in a game before this. I've played previous cs, call of duty, dead by daylight, just to name a few bad ones. But Counter Strike 2 has a serious problem with it. Its almost every game and that's not a joke. Imagine a cheater in every round in a different game. You'd lose your fucking mind. Well that's exactly whats happening here. The stuff people say and do in this game you honestly can't make up. Some [i]fun[/i] ones:

1. Pretty blatant cheater on the opposing team, a member of our own team notices this and starts cheating blatantly himself, so it ends up in a cheater v cheater (which may sound fun and all but I genuinely want to improve in the game, so how am I suppose to do this?) and the opposing cheater starts advertising his cheats in the chat like wtf?.

2. A different group of players. A person on the opposing team is cheating (this is after multiple loses and just a bad day on the game in general.) 2 people on my own team ask me and my friend for permission for them to rage hack back. Like what the hell do you even say to that??. Its like everyone has cheats and are just ready to blow their load with them. After a couple of rounds of this, THE GAME ACTUALLY ENDED. Like we got a message saying someone in the match was cheating and it got cancelled. And I sat there pondering that for a second and thought "how is this the first time I've seen this in 2 weeks of me playing against these ppl?". 

Its soooo baddddd. Its almost put me off the game completely. How am I suppose to improve let alone enjoy the game when every match is being ruined by cheaters on BOTH teams? And some of the stuff these cheaters do, like how is it not being flagged instantly? Some rounds feel as though there isn't an anti-cheat.
