text:
This product is a glorified gambling casino, and I CANNOT consciously recommend it knowing that Valve is ACTIVELY exploiting underage children just to make a quick buck. Coffeezilla made a couple of videos on this subject—go check them out: https://youtu.be/13eiDhuvM6Y?si=FYQd2EsI5bxub95Y

First off, let’s start with the price: this game is free, which means anyone can redeem it, own it, and play it—even underage kids. The whole game revolves around case openings and cosmetic trading (a.k.a. "skins"), which hold real value in the Steam community market. You can sell these skins to receive Steam credit and use it to buy games or even a Steam Deck.

A case costs around €1.50. You can get one for free by leveling up your in-game experience or playing every week—but only if you purchase a €15 premium pass that allows you to participate in "competitive" matches (more on that later). To open these boxes, you need to buy an additional key, which costs €2.50. Once you open the case, you will see—and I’m not kidding—a roulette wheel spinning with a ticking sound that makes the experience more addictive and engaging, showing you which cosmetic you will receive. The prizes you win usually won’t reimburse the cost of the case-opening experience: most of the time, the game gives you a 10-cent cosmetic that you can sell for half the price on the market, netting you a mere 3 cents of profit—if you can even call it that. Valuable skins are extremely rare.

There’s no ID verification process for this entire system. This means that children can buy, open, and sell cases or skins on the Steam market. Since they cannot technically cash out the money they make from selling items on Steam, this is considered "not gambling." Valve is exploiting a loophole in legislation to target children and profit from them. Everything else—the "gameplay"—is just window dressing to disguise this as an actual game.

The competitive aspect of this "game" is a complete joke. There is no effective anti-cheat system, and the matchmaking algorithm is laughable. If you have friends, you might occasionally have some fun and stand a chance. Otherwise, you’ll constantly face full teams while you're stuck with random players who don’t communicate—or worse, players who shout slurs and use the N-word. The game rewards people with low ping or cheats because—surprise, SURPRISE—there’s virtually no anti-cheat system. You’ll frequently encounter players spin-botting or firing five sniper shots in one second. Don’t believe me? Watch any high-rank CS2 streamer: you can’t play a high-ELO tier game without running into at least one cheater. Reporting them is almost useless—it’s extremely rare for anyone to get banned. Adding to this is the issue of developers forgetting to disable debug features after updates, which has allowed players to discover in-game commands that grant access to developer tools—essentially wall hacks that let you see enemies through walls.

The gameplay itself (I refuse to call this a game) is atrocious. It feels slow and unresponsive. If you get hit, you’re "teleported" back by a few inches, messing up your aim and crosshair positioning. Enemies feel like bullet sponges, taking forever to kill, while you can get one-tapped—even with full armor—from two miles away by a pistol. The game heavily favors players with lower ping. Counter-Strike 2: Where VAC Stands for Very Acceptable Cheating"

Ah, CS2. The long-awaited evolution of CS:GO that we’ve all been waiting for—because who doesn’t want to see blatant cheaters have a field day while the so-called “anti-cheat” pretends to take a nap?

Let’s talk about VAC (Valve Anti-Cheat), the superhero we neither asked for nor deserve. It’s like a mall security guard trying to stop a bank heist by looking the other way. Wall hacks? No problem. Shooting through smoke like they’ve got built-in X-ray vision? VAC's got this—oh wait, no, it doesn’t. And my personal favorite: sniping while mid-air like they're auditioning for The Matrix Reloaded. Seriously, Valve, are you even trying?

I’ve been watching some of these cheaters for six weeks straight. Six. Weeks. That’s 42 days of “investigating” accounts that are as subtle as a flashing neon sign reading “I’M CHEATING.” And yet, their accounts are still active, merrily ruining games for the rest of us. At this point, VAC isn’t an anti-cheat; it’s an anti-player system.

But hey, maybe Valve has a grand strategy here. Why bother fixing the problem when you can just sell another shiny skin and make bank? Who cares about gameplay integrity when there’s money to be made, right? Because clearly, keeping the cheaters happy is the real endgame.

I’ve been playing Counter-Strike for over six years, and the cheating issue has gone from bad to comically worse. At least in CS:GO, there was some pretense of trying. With CS2, Valve has just leaned into the chaos, like, “Cheating? Meh, let the community deal with it. We’re busy counting our Steam Deck profits.”

So, if you’re considering picking up CS2, just know that the real game isn’t “Counter-Strike.” It’s “Guess Who’s Cheating This Match!” Pro tip: it’s probably half the server.

Valve, congratulations. You’ve somehow managed to take a legendary franchise and turn it into a glorified aimbot showcase. Bravo. Clap. Clap. Clap.

text:
Counter-Strike 2 is the latest installment in the iconic FPS series, and it quickly proves why it remains one of the most important titles in the history of competitive multiplayer games. While the game does have issues with optimization and dealing with cheaters, it still offers incredible dynamics, deep competition, and immense satisfaction in every round played.

Gameplay and Dynamics:
Counter-Strike 2 stays true to the series’ roots, offering fast-paced matches that require not only quick reflexes but also solid tactics. The core gameplay remains unchanged – it’s still a shooter where every move, every shot, and every decision counts. The classic maps are back, and the game revolves around the familiar setup: terrorists vs. counter-terrorists. Every round is a fight for survival, and victory hinges on teamwork and precise shooting. The in-game economy, where players earn money based on their round performance, adds depth, requiring careful resource management.

New Features and Improvements:
Counter-Strike 2 brings noticeable improvements in visuals – the graphics are much more detailed, and the game engine allows for better lighting and shadow effects, enhancing the overall aesthetic experience. Though the changes are subtle, they bring a fresh layer of immersion to the classic gameplay formula. The animations for characters and smoother transitions between different elements of the map further improve the feel of the game. These details make the game look fresh while still staying true to the spirit of the original Counter-Strike.

Optimization Issues and Cheater Problems:
Unfortunately, like many AAA games, Counter-Strike 2 struggles with optimization, especially on lower-end systems. Despite updates, some players still experience frame drops and performance issues that can affect the gaming experience. While this is likely to be addressed in future patches, it may be frustrating for some players.

Another ongoing issue is the presence of cheaters. Although Valve takes action to minimize cheaters in the game, some players still use unfair methods, which can negatively affect the gameplay experience. The VAC (Valve Anti-Cheat) system is in place, but there are still instances where cheating impacts the quality of matches.

Summary:
Counter-Strike 2 is still one of the best FPS games out there, providing thrilling, fast-paced gameplay and immense satisfaction from winning rounds. Despite some issues with optimization and cheaters, the game still offers a lot of fun, and for many players, it’s an essential title. If you’re looking for intense, team-based competition and great fun in the classic style, Counter-Strike 2 will certainly meet your expectations.

text:
CS has always had a cheating problem, but when I say it's bad now, it really is. For new players, and my own experience 200hrs in, you can expect the following:
Playing casual until rank 3, not uncommon to see cheaters, sometimes they get kicked, sometimes not.
Grind competitive games until rank 10, where you will encounter cheaters (obvious ones with bhop, spin, aim, wall) on average atleast 1/3 games. And if that's not enough for you to lose motivation to continue then surely bad teammates or flat out griefers will make your day!
Don't forget that after about 2 levels worth of xp you will start receiving a reduction in XP! This is surely with the intention of reducing smurfing which can be a positive, but feels very demotivating when you're just trying to get into the actual game. (Premier). And considering the state of competitive, even less enticing.
Buying Prime in reality makes very little difference as most cheaters buy accounts which already have the game unlocked. But still, is something that you yourself will eventually need.
When you eventually push through to Rank 10(lvl) and are ready to step into Premier I'm sorry to tell you but the cheating problem does not end there. Although it gets less and less common as you start to climb up (presumably because they actually get banned), the only problem being that making it all the way here for a new player seems quite unlikely due to how exhausting it is to actually get to start [i]Playing the game. [/i]
Speaking of bans, although countless of reports I have only seen 2 super obvious cheaters get VAC banned ingame, nullifying the match. A stronger anti-cheat, as well as reparations for affected legit players who are found to have played with/against cheaters in the past would make the game so much more enjoyable and fair.
---
Besides the huge cheating problems, some improvements that i'd love to see is:
- The ability to surrender games, even if no one has left.
This might go against the competitive nature of the game, but the fact is that you will far to often have teammates that give up, players who get kicked due to many reasons, face cheaters or flat out just get stomped. Instead of forcing you to sit through a super boring game with no absolute way of winning, just let the team come to a unanimous vote to accept defeat early.
- Larger competitive map pool.
The game can feel very repetitive, especially as some maps are far more favored then others.
- More active engagement from Valve
Altough CS is one of the biggest games right now, and has been for so long. There is an underwhelming amount of response from Valve.
I understand that they might not want to touch the games meta to much, but simultaneously there is a bunch of things in the game that could be optimized, tweaked and improved. Clunky mechanics, map object hitboxes not corresponding to visual elements, and so on.
It feels like the dev team behind the game is like a small indie company, or rather that the people at the office prefer working on other games, and that CS is kind of the forgotten middle child.
---
Will I continue to play? Absolutely, Is it because the game Is GOOD?... No, I just like to suffer and argue with people online.

text:
I have been playing this game since Counter-Strike 1.1 or 1.2, when only locally, without any Internet, you could show your skills, reaction and intelligence (the Siege map was the first). Of course, in closed computer clubs there was no option to use cheats, everyone was equal. After that, several updates took place, and on version 1.6, an online mode appeared, where you could sit at home and choose a server with the lowest ping to give yourself completely. 
However, technology is developing and this became a reason for the emergence of cheaters. In those days, server owners themselves took care of protection from cheaters. Before connecting to the server, the anti-cheat had to be launched, which minimized the game on unequal terms. I trained well, bought myself the top equipment at that time - the MX-518 mouse, then the G-500 from Logitech, a SteelSeries mousepad with a picture of SK-gaming, which still serves me faithfully and truly...
After that, with marriage, the birth of a son and work, I abandoned Counter-Strike for several years. I definitely missed the version of Source and Go (not completely).
My son was growing up, I often told him that I played Counter-Strike, went to competitions within my country and was quite successful. He started playing CS GO. But as soon as he learned how to do this, the version of CS-2 came out. He, having my account with medals for 10 years of merit, began to play very well (in my opinion) and I had to buy him a computer to play Faceit - with support for the TPM2.0 module, etc.
This winter of 2024, we decided that it would be nice to play together on cold winter evenings as a father and son. I really wanted to spend time with him, learn something from him and teach him some skills, tactics and strategies. Moreover, I did not miss a single major championship and definitely saw and knew the nuances of the game in a team - economics, throwing grenades, psychological balance. So I got out my old but productive computer and upgraded it - it was a Xeon 2678v3 with 32 gigabytes of DDR3 in 4-channel mode. I bought myself an RTX-1660 super video card, an M.2 SSD drive, a 180 Hz monitor and was ready to surprise my son. I had to create a second Steam account and buy Prime for $ 15 in the hope that I would bypass cheaters and honestly show my game. But I was extremely negatively surprised when after purchasing Prime I had to level up to level 10 to get into the Premier game. Due to my busy schedule and playing only in the evenings for 2-3 hours, it took me about two weeks. I don't understand why a former pro player needs such tests? On the way to the Premier game, I encountered cheaters in 80 percent of cases, both on my team and on the enemy team. It was a real test. I thought that when I get access to the Premier mode, especially since I bought it for money, I will exclude the possibility of playing with cheaters or against them. But this was a mistake - no one from Valve is looking for cheaters or monitoring them. There are even more of them in the Premier mode than in the training mode.
I was very disappointed, for the paid mode I got the same number of cheaters in the game as for the regular mode. It's terrible.
I understand Valve's financial policy - to receive tens and hundreds of thousands of dollars for colorful knives. This is a good profit, unlike a good game. I am very sorry to state the fact that such a great game with a long history can ruin talented players who could become champions. Alas, they will have to go to other games, where the developers are more concerned about fair play, like the Olympic Games.
At the moment, I do not recommend this game, especially I do not recommend paying money for it.

I am sure that with such an approach from the creators - this game will disappear forever...

Alas, but I must admit this fact...

Alright, here it comes. After my modest playtime through CS 1.6, CS source, CS:GO and CS2, I think I can base my opinion to finally rate this game. CS:GO was the perfect game for me, from the map design and networking to the satisfying sound of the guns. That changed with CS2. Don't get me wrong, it's still a good game, but it has many, many flaws that CS:GO did not have. I'm talking about the gameplay and networking. How did you break the game? Why does my connection have to be routed through a random country to get 100 more ms in ping? Why does damage prediction even exist? I stop shooting after I see a ragdolled enemy lying on the floor and then get 1 tapped by a ghost? And this happens countless times.

And the cheater problem... I'm not saying CS:GO was better in terms of  anticheat or anything, but for a company that makes billions in revenue of a single game, its just unacceptable to have that many cheaters. 
And it's not even soft cheating like wallhack and radar, it's straight up spinbotting and aimhacking. There is no fun at all. Why does FACEIT, a third party, get a better anticheat system?

Said that, I'll still pour hundreds of hours more into this game, because I love to onetap and I'm a bit of a masochist myself. But it could be so much better. So much.

text:
[b]Counter-Strike 2: A Chaotic Rollercoaster of Hope and Disappointment[/b]

[b]CS2's recoil[/b] is like a [i]blindfolded octopus having a seizure[/i]. You think you’ve got the spray down after hours of practice, but then the bullets start doing their own thing like they’ve got a personal vendetta against you. At this point, I’ve given up trying to control it. Now, I just [b]spray and pray[/b]. It’s like my mouse is in a fight with my gun, and neither of them is winning. It’s like chess, but the pawns scream at you in Russian and accuse you of cheating. 10/10.

[u]Left/Right Hand Switch[/u]
So, I had this dream… of having my knife in my left hand and my guns in the right. Simple, right? [strike]Wrong[/strike]. There’s no console bind for it, and when I try to use a config to make the switch, the game resets my visual effects. Now I’m stuck with my knife on the right and a broken heart on the left. Thanks, Valve. You really [i]nailed[/i] it. Tried to throw a grenade through a window; it bounced back and killed me. My teammates have been laughing for three hours. 11/10.

[u]Fullscreen Mode[/u]
Fullscreen mode in CS2 is like trying to fit an elephant through a mouse hole. It’s buggy, glitchy, and somehow leaves you wondering if you’ve accidentally opened a portal to another dimension. The screen flickers more than my hope for a clean kill, and if you’re lucky, your mouse might just disappear altogether. But hey, at least it's consistent—like a bad relationship.

[u]Subtick System[/u]
Ah, the [b]subtick system[/b]. Supposed to fix tickrate issues, right? Well, it’s like Valve hired a magician to fix lag but instead just conjured up more confusion. My bullets might as well be magic spells because they rarely hit where I aim. It’s 64-tick, but it feels like a downgrade from 128, and no amount of sub-ticks can fix that. The bullets are on vacation, and I’m still here trying to shoot ghosts. I’m not sure who’s having a worse time—me, or the game itself. Finally got into Premier mode, only to be told by a 12-year-old my aim was worse than his grandma's. Best FPS experience.

[b]Smoke Grenades[/b]
The new smoke grenades are amazing—until someone shoots through them, and I realize I’m out in the open like a clown. 9/10, would panic again. Valve really improved the graphics… now if only they could work some magic on my aim to make it as sharp as my screen.

[b]Weapon Skins[/b]
Spent three hours customizing my weapon skins. Didn't shoot anyone because I was too busy admiring them. Best museum simulator ever! Every match is a mix of genius strategies and utter chaos. Mostly chaos. 10/10 would flashbang my team again.

[spoiler]Final Thoughts[/spoiler]
So, if you like a chaotic mix of hope, confusion, and unrealized dreams, then CS2 is for you. It’s fun, but [u]not[/u] for the reasons you think. The smokes are realistic, the gameplay is tight, and my teammates still call me 'bot.' Some things never change. CS2: Come for the tactical gameplay, stay for the existential dread after your fifth deagle whiff. If you want to feel like a tactical genius and an absolute clown in the same 30 seconds, this is the game for you. 10/10 would spray like a firehose again.

[quote=Kakashii666][code]CS2: Come for the tactical gameplay, stay for the existential dread after your fifth deagle whiff[/code]
[code]CS2 perfectly captures the feeling of being a genius and a complete fool, all within 30 seconds. It’s not a shooter; it’s a psychological thriller where you’re the joke[/code]
[code]The smokes are realistic, the gameplay is sharp, and my teammates still shout 'bot' every time I miss. Some things are timeless, like my incompetence[/code]
[code]It’s like chess, but the pawns are on energy drinks, scream at you in Russian, and accuse you of cheating—while one of them is probably wall-hacking. 10/10 tactical chaos[/code]
[code]CS2: Where every match is a beautiful mess of strategies, skill, and flashbangs—mostly flashbangs[/code]
[code]Valve really nailed the graphics, but no amount of detail can cover up my panic when I’m staring down a corner, praying I don’t get knifed[/code]
[code]Counter-Strike 2: The game that makes you question your life choices, your aim, and whether it’s even possible to play without getting flashbanged by your own team[/code]
[code]The new smoke grenades are revolutionary… until you realize they’re the perfect cover for your teammates to ‘accidentally’ shoot you in the back. Classic CS2[/code]

If you thought the gameplay and matchmaking issues were bad, just wait until you encounter CS2's thriving population of cheaters. This game isn’t just a playground for hackers—it’s their personal kingdom, where they run unchecked and unchallenged. Aimbots, wallhacks, spinbots—you name it, and you’ll see it in almost every match. What’s worse is that Valve doesn’t seem to care.

VAC: A Dinosaur of Anti-Cheat Systems
Valve Anti-Cheat (VAC) is the same antiquated system they’ve been parading around for years, and it’s utterly useless in Counter-Strike 2. Cheaters laugh at it as they blatantly ruin match after match. VAC bans, if they ever come, happen weeks after the damage is done—long enough for the cheater to create a new account and start the cycle all over again. It’s not just ineffective; it’s insulting.

A Cheater's Paradise
Cheaters have become so rampant in CS2 that it feels like they outnumber legitimate players in ranked matches. The sheer audacity of some of these hackers—openly mocking their opponents while flaunting their cheats—shows just how toothless Valve’s response is. Even in supposedly "high-rank" games, the presence of cheaters destroys any sense of competition or fairness.

False Promises and Empty Words
Valve promised improvements to anti-cheat for CS2, but what we got is a hollow PR statement with zero tangible results. If anything, the situation has worsened. Features like kernel-level anti-cheat, used by competitors like Riot’s Vanguard, aren’t even on the table. Instead, players are left to report cheaters manually, which feels like screaming into the void.

Impact on the Community
The cheater infestation has turned the once-loyal Counter-Strike community into a bitter, disillusioned group. Legitimate players are abandoning the game in droves, leaving only the cheaters and those masochistic enough to endure this broken experience. CS2’s potential for competitive play has been utterly destroyed by Valve’s negligence.

Counter-Strike 2 isn’t just failing to deal with cheaters—it’s actively enabling them. At this point, calling the game “unplayable” is generous. Valve’s refusal to take anti-cheat measures seriously is the ultimate betrayal to its player base. This isn’t just a problem—it’s a catastrophe.

1. Improved Graphics: The Source 2 engine elevates the visuals significantly. Maps feel more alive with better lighting, textures, and environmental details, while still maintaining the clean design essential for competitive gameplay.

Cons:

1. Optimization Issues: While the visuals are stunning, some players report performance drops even on high-end hardware. Optimization needs further tweaking.

2. Lack of New Content: At launch, the game primarily updates existing CS:GO maps and mechanics rather than introducing substantial new content, leaving some players wanting more.

3. Cheating Concerns: Despite Valve’s anti-cheat improvements, the game still faces issues with hackers, particularly in casual and lower-ranked matches.

4. Steep Learning Curve: As with its predecessors, Counter-Strike 2 is not beginner-friendly. New players might struggle with the mechanics and the unforgiving nature of competitive play.

5. Community Issues: Toxicity remains a significant problem, especially in public lobbies and lower-ranked matches.

text:
=====================
Matchmaking
=====================
Negatives:
Yes, there are quite a bit of cheaters in this game. Now I'm a new account so my experience probably will be different than most, but I encounter a cheater about once ever 5 games. However, that's the only big issue I see with the game's matchmaking.


=====================
Gameplay
=====================
Positives:
I think this is where Counter Strike is unrivaled. The base gameplay is incredible. It takes a while to learn the shooting mechanics, however, once you do, it is incredibly satisfying. Aside from that though, there are so many community made maps that allow you to play gamemodes that aren't just competitive 5v5. Many of these also allow you to build up your skills while having fun.

One of my personal favorites is KZ. It's basically parkour and it takes a while to get used to it, but once you do, it's incredibly fun. While you likely won't be performing moves quite as difficult as in KZ, it's very useful for learning the movement mechanics and performing skill jumps on certain maps to get into unexpected positions.

Overall, the game is very simple, however, there's so much depth to the mechanics.

Negatives:
The game isn't the most intuitive starting off. You have to do a lot of searching yourself for how to do things. A big one is utility. The game itself only just added a barebones system to teach how to throw utility. To really learn, you have to watch either YouTube videos or download practice maps that tell you the different lineups.

There is also a lot of memorization. I personally enjoy it, but that's because I'm crazy. Probably the most prevalent mechanic that requires is shooting. While you can tap shoot and burst fire very easily, to fully spray, you need to memorize a set pattern. This is important if you want to climb the ranks. Utility is also another point of memorization. If you don't know Utility in this game, it becomes very difficult to do anything without getting shot in the head from angles you couldn't even see.

 
=====================
Community
=====================
Positives:
Very few games can rival the amount of community made content that Counter Strike has. There's so many different community gamemodes you can join in the server browser. There's so many different tools for learning the game with custom maps. There are also a lot of cool people I've played with. It's not every game, but overall, I don't run into many people being toxic or saying slurs, although the slurs definitely do occur.

Negatives:
Slurs and cheating.


=====================
Summary
=====================
The base gameplay is very rewarding with a ton of depth. There are also many community gamemodes which many also reinforce the mechanics needed to improve in the game. There are also a lot of kind players who make the experience better.

However, there are quite a few cheaters and also some games have slurs being said a lot.

You can see Valve's anti-cheat measures with some random waves of bans and tweaks to the system, but there seems to be an apparent lack of transparency with which progress is being made, where players have to ask whether these are meaningful steps or just a show. 
The Premier ranking system is like some mathematical joke. Rising to 10,000 feels like this utterly cruel grind, where losses hurt a lot more than wins help. My experience puts a very bleak picture: getting to 3,000 was a lot harder last season. getting to 10,000 now seems to be almost perfect play and accepting all the chaos of matchmaking. Solo queuers are up against stacked teams with really inconsistent teammate skills and a points economy that seems quite rigged against any real progress. 
New things like dynamic smokes and sub-tick updates show ambition, but the resulting execution has created problems. Dying behind cover or getting traded in a way that defies logic makes anyone lose faith in the very engine. Meanwhile, the community's ire keeps simmering in the form of clips of phantom bullets. But there are some rays of brilliance-the reworked maps allow for different strategies, and the gunplay stays sharp at its core as long as the netcode doesn't act upd.

I cannot recommend this game to anyone. It is just a complete waste of your time and full of cheaters.

I played Counter-Strike some twenty years ago. I have played other shooters in between, and when I returned to Counter-Strike for bit of Nostalgia... Well, you need to relearn the old ropes, get rid of the rust, but over all it is not that hard to get a hang of things. But in the process of doing so, I did not score very high on the premier or competitive modes. Therefore, my rank remains as silver, and that is so even if I am able to outperform people with various shades of blue as their rank in a match. The internet is full of people who claim to be hardstuck in ELO hell, and I have to admit to being yet another addition among their endless ranks. But what may set me aside from the rest that within these 400 hours of gameplay, and estimated of around 800 matches, I have had a grand total of five (5) matches without a single cheater.

Therefore, the reason I cannot escape the ELO Hell is due to the rampant cheating done in this game, and I have noticed a pattern that repeats. I get put into game with cheaters, I watch the demo afterwards, I report them on both teams and eventually after a month or two my trust factor seems to improve and all of a sudden I get placed into a match without a single cheater. The problem here is, I have gotten used to playing against people who see through walls, people who I have reported for cheating and who have gone to reach 35k+ in Premier mode. Therefore, I will outperform your average genuine silvers by a long mile, and hence they will naturally just mass report me for cheating. And since my performance in these matches is likely considerably higher than my normal K/D of around one (1), it would appear quite alarming indeed for the VAC system. Therefore, my trust factor plummets, I get thrown back into the endless loop of matches with those blatant cheaters, and naturally the VAC will attempt to catch me for the suspected cheating that I am not doing. Such as drastically increasing the spread of my guns, so that even while completely still, and crouching, I will have no idea where the bullets will fly. Or perhaps it will simply move my aim on its own to about an inch to the right away from the enemy, which will get me killed in a gunfight. There have even been times where the game has not even rendered enemy players on my screen in order to check if I am using a wall hack, or something, which then gets me killed and the team has some choice of words about my blindness. Then you got the sudden and random freezes, when these things get applied, never mind the utterly unreliable jitter than renders the game if not outright unplayable, then at least like a badly made stop-motion movie. 

And what makes it most irksome, is that in order to even see how you compare with rest of the world in CS2, you need to have a premier rating higher than 4k, which then puts you to around the bottom 99%. But that is not the whole truth, because in September of 2024, around 10% of all players had ranking below 4k. Almost 20% of all players had a ranking below 5k. I imagine these numbers to be fairly similar even today. Therefore, you cannot even reliably compare yourself with other players. As neither can you just disable the rank changes and information entirely, nor does the game offer you a chance to just play 5v5 matches without some sort of pointless ranking system. It would probably bother me much less to be pitted against cheaters if I had no clue whatsoever how the end result of the match would affect my rating. I know it is going to remain as silver, so why waste my time by showing +100 or -100 points? Heck, it could just show: "???" for me and I would be a much happier player.

Additionally, the thing the Devs of this game should add is simply a "Rage" mode, with its own ranking as per Premier mode. You can toggle on the cheats you want to use, and then the matchmaking finds people with the same cheats active for you to play with. If someone has more cheats active, then the same cheats get activated for everyone else as well. People cheat in CS2, they always will, but by creating a way for them to cheat legally and without a need for third party software, you would actually reduce the potential customer base for these cheat developers. Why pay hundreds of dollars, when you just queue for free and play against other cheaters, without ruining the experience for all the people who want to play without cheats? 

So yeah, I cannot recommend this game for anyone. It is just too full of cheaters.

text:
A Great Time Sink. 
This game is incredibly addictive. At first, you climb up to Global Elite, but then your ranks get reset. They add a Premier mode where every second game at high ranks is against cheaters. I’d say it’s either with them or against them; however, in the last 30 games, I can’t recall having cheaters on my side -only against me, including a whole bunch of spinbots.

The CS2 community consists of people who are dissatisfied with life. I can understand them; after all, not many stick around in this game for 3, 5, or even 11 years. The game truly makes a person its slave, but unfortunately, the skills you gain in it can’t really be applied in real life.

It’s a great way to waste the precious time given to you in life. I really enjoyed the Broken Fang and Shattered Web operations, but it’s been a while since anything similar came out. Not to mention the fluctuating tick rate with inconsistent headshot hits. I remember when we played Faceit instead of CS GO, precisely because the 128 tick rate felt so much better than the 64 tick rate in matchmaking. Now, I’m at a loss for words...

In CS GO (The previous version), the occasional VAC bans and the Overwatch system gave a sense of security, and the number of cheaters fluctuated. Unfortunately, in CS2, it seems that has completely disappeared. Dozens of private cheats work flawlessly without a single ban (I won’t name them, but avid players know exactly what I’m talking about).

But there are, of course, positives. One can’t be that critical, obviously. The first positive is the networking atmosphere. The community brings together people my age, a bit younger, but sometimes even older, who speak an absolutely countless number of languages. It’s a great way to practice a language for free when you’re in a non-English-speaking environment, for example.

After all, it’s good for reaction training and fostering a competitive spirit.

There’s a full-fledged market with its ups and downs - mostly ups, of course. I remember being young and watching people with AWP Dragon Lore (Factory New) for $1000, marveling at how an in-game item could be worth such unimaginable money. I even had an AK-47 Vulcan (Factory New) for a whopping $50 and an AWP Graphite for $15. Don’t even get me started on the Katowice 2014 Holo stickers for $0.50! Such items have grown more than Bitcoin.

Overall, I’d call this another chapter - the old good CS. But I advise young people to think carefully while your time hasn’t run out. I would return and play it again, but not now, being a healthy and full-of-life man. This game is a great way to greet old age.

Thank you to the game for all the bad and good it brought into my life.

There is always a choice, and everyone makes it for themselves.

Jumping into Counter-Strike 2, I felt like a kid in a candy store. The crisp graphics, refined mechanics, and the sheer thrill of tactical play—it's a gamer’s paradise. As a new player, I was ready to immerse myself in this legendary FPS (First-Person Shooter) and climb the ranks. Everything was set for an epic journey.

Then, reality struck hard. I quickly discovered that Prime matchmaking, the promised land of fair play, was plagued by cheaters. Encountering hackers who used wallhacks, aimbots, and various other nefarious tools was an all-too-frequent frustration. Matches became less about skill and strategy and more about spotting the cheater on the other team. It was disheartening, to say the least.

Despite these hurdles, the core of Counter-Strike 2 remains robust and engaging. The adrenaline rush of a well-coordinated team effort, the satisfaction of a perfectly executed headshot, and the deep sense of camaraderie in teamwork are still very much alive. But these positive experiences are constantly overshadowed by the unfair advantage cheaters bring to the table.

Valve has implemented anti-cheat systems, but they seem to fall short against the relentless tide of new hacks. It’s a game that holds immense potential but needs stronger, more effective measures to keep the playing field level. If Valve can crack down on cheating more aggressively, Counter-Strike 2 could easily become the ultimate tactical FPS experience. Until then, it’s a bittersweet affair for new players stepping into this iconic game.

text:
Gameplay (7/10)
Let’s start with the good: the core gameplay of Counter-Strike is still here, and it’s as addictive as ever. The tactical gunplay, the economy system, and the emphasis on teamwork are all intact, and when everything clicks, there’s nothing quite like it. The new "sub-tick" system is a welcome improvement, making the game feel more responsive and precise.

But here’s the problem: it’s still Counter-Strike. If you’ve played CS:GO, you’ve essentially played CS2. The changes feel incremental at best, and while the sub-tick system is nice, it doesn’t fundamentally change the experience. For a game that’s been in development for years, it’s disappointing how little innovation there is. It’s like Valve took CS:GO, gave it a facelift, and called it a day.

Graphics and Sound (8/10)
Visually, CS2 is a step up from CS:GO, thanks to the Source 2 engine. The lighting is better, the textures are sharper, and the maps look more detailed. But let’s be honest—this isn’t a groundbreaking visual overhaul. It’s an improvement, but it’s not exactly cutting-edge by 2023 standards.

The sound design, on the other hand, is excellent. The audio cues are crisp and directional, which is crucial for gameplay. But again, this is just a slightly polished version of what CS:GO already did well. It’s hard to get excited about something that feels like it should have been in the game years ago.

Maps and Content (6/10)
CS2 launched with a handful of reworked classic maps, and while they look better, they’re still the same maps we’ve been playing for over a decade. Where are the new maps? Where’s the fresh content? It feels like Valve is resting on its laurels, relying on nostalgia rather than pushing the series forward.

The lack of new content is especially frustrating when you consider how long CS2 was in development. For a game that’s supposed to be a major upgrade, it feels like a missed opportunity to breathe new life into the franchise.

Cheaters: The Elephant in the Room (3/10)
Here’s the biggest issue with CS2: the cheaters. Oh, the cheaters. It’s absolutely rampant, and it’s ruining the experience. Every other match seems to have someone with suspiciously perfect aim or an uncanny ability to know exactly where you are at all times. Valve’s anti-cheat system, VAC, is a joke at this point. It’s like trying to stop a flood with a paper towel.

The prevalence of cheaters makes competitive matches feel like a coin flip. Will you get a fair game, or will you be stuck playing against someone who’s clearly using hacks? It’s infuriating, and it’s driving players away. Valve needs to take this issue seriously, because right now, it’s a black mark on an otherwise great game.

Performance and Accessibility (8/10)
On the technical side, CS2 runs well on a variety of systems, which is a plus. The Source 2 engine is optimized, and even players with older hardware can enjoy the game. However, the learning curve is still steep, and while Valve has added some new tutorials, it’s not enough to make the game truly accessible to newcomers. If you’re not already a Counter-Strike fan, CS2 can feel like an impenetrable fortress.

Monetization (7/10)
CS2’s monetization is… fine. It’s free-to-play, which is great, but the microtransactions are still there. Weapon skins, cases, and the dreaded loot boxes are all present and accounted for. While these don’t affect gameplay, the reliance on gambling mechanics feels exploitative, especially when you consider how much money some players sink into cosmetics.

Conclusion
Counter-Strike 2 is a game I love, but it’s also a game that drives me crazy. It’s still Counter-Strike at its core, and that’s both its greatest strength and its biggest weakness. The lack of innovation, the cheater problem, and the underwhelming amount of new content make it hard to fully recommend. And yet, I keep coming back. There’s something about the gameplay that’s just irresistible, even when it’s infuriating.

Overall Rating: 6.5/10
CS2 is a flawed gem. It’s a game I can’t quit, but it’s also a game that constantly tests my patience. If Valve can address the cheater problem and add more meaningful content, it could be amazing. Until then, it’s a love-hate relationship—emphasis on the hate.

text:
Alright, let’s really get into it, because if I’m going to lose my sanity over Counter-Strike 2, I might as well take you all down with me.

CS2 is a special breed of madness. It’s like Valve decided to take all the rage-inducing aspects of life—traffic jams, waiting at the DMV, finding out your favorite show got canceled—and wrapped it up in a tactical shooter where pressing the “W” key is an uncrackable enigma for 50% of your teammates. It’s a masterpiece, honestly.

Let’s break it down, starting with the Russian Comrades.

First of all, shout-out to the Russians. Somehow, every single game has that one player named Daniil_Dragonov69 who is determined to relive the glory days of CS 1.6. If there’s a language barrier, don’t worry—they’ve got their trusty arsenal of swear words and insults that can pierce through any linguistic barrier. It’s a bonding experience, really. You know the game is about to hit peak levels of chaos when the chat lights up with, “idi nahui” followed by seven exclamation points.

And don’t get me wrong, not every Russian player is a harbinger of chaos. But when they are? Oh boy. You’ve got Viktor, who never leaves spawn because he’s too busy arguing with Sergey over how their dog could probably frag harder than you. Sergey, meanwhile, is five shots deep in vodka and has decided that rushing B every round with a P90 is the only viable strat. Who are you to question the ancient CS2 wisdom that has been passed down through the annals of Russian matchmaking lore?

But let’s not put all the blame on our Cyrillic-speaking comrades, because we’ve got a whole zoo of teammates to deal with.

Enter the Braindead Squad™.

There’s a special kind of agony reserved for those moments when you realize your team has collectively forgotten the basic mechanics of a first-person shooter. There’s Larry, who still hasn’t figured out that the mouse controls where you aim. Watching him play is like watching a nature documentary on sloths—fascinatingly slow, but with an undercurrent of existential dread. You’re screaming internally (and maybe externally), “Dude, just point and click! It’s like taking a picture with your phone, but the photo is of the enemy’s imminent demise!”

Then there’s Ricky, who apparently has an allergy to the “W” key. I don’t know what happened in Ricky’s past to make him so afraid of moving forward, but it’s clearly a trauma he needs to work through. Watching Ricky play is like watching someone learn how to walk for the first time—he hesitates, he stumbles, and by the time he decides to move, the entire enemy team has already rotated, planted, taken a smoke break, and ordered takeout.

Let’s not forget Barry, whose reaction times make a 100-year-old grandma look like Usain Bolt on Red Bull. You’ll ping a location, call out “enemy to your left!” and Barry will spin around like he’s the protagonist in an old Western showdown—except instead of pulling the trigger, he’s contemplating life, the universe, and whether he left the oven on. By the time Barry’s turned 180 degrees, the enemy has not only killed him, but probably wrote a small novel about it and sent it to Barry’s Kindle.

The Voice Comms & The Panic

When you’re playing CS2, voice comms are a minefield of emotions. Half the time, you’re giving tactical advice to a team that’s ignoring you in favor of making sandwich orders. You’ve got one guy who’s breathing so hard into his mic, you’re worried he’s going to pass out, another one with their TV on so loud you’re getting live updates on some random sports match, and then there’s that one guy who’s literally just screaming into the void every time he dies.

“WHY IS NOBODY WATCHING MID?!”
“DUDE, YOU RAN PAST HIM!”
“I SAID SMOKE, NOT FLASH! HOW DID YOU EVEN MIX THAT UP?!”

At this point, you’re more like a therapist than a player. You’re soothing one teammate who’s threatening to uninstall, calming down another who’s rage-bought an AWP with zero cash left, and trying not to lose your own mind in the process.

Cheaters: The Boss Fight You Never Asked For

But the real kicker is the cheaters. These guys are like the final boss in a game, except there’s no pattern to learn and no weakness to exploit. You’re just stuck watching them pull off inhuman flick shots, walking through walls, and doing 360-degree no-scopes like it’s a TikTok challenge.

And what makes it worse is the false hope you get every single time. You see their sketchy movement, their aim that seems oddly precise, and you’re like, “No, maybe they’re just good.” But then you spectate them and realize this guy has hacked the actual Matrix. He’s playing on a level that even the game’s own anti-cheat system is staring at, blinking confusedly, like, “Wait, is this allowed?”

The Report Button of Hope

You press that report button like it’s going to send a flare up to Valve headquarters, alerting them that there’s a cheater in their midst. In reality, that report is probably going straight into a queue the length of a CVS receipt. It’s like shouting into a black hole and expecting a polite response back. “Oh, you’ve reported a cheater? Good luck, we’ll get back to you in 2032.”

Why We Keep Playing

And yet, despite all of this, CS2 remains undefeated as the ultimate test of endurance. It’s a battle of patience, willpower, and possibly your soul. There’s something about the absolute chaos, the feeling of pulling off a clutch play, or even the satisfaction of getting a lucky headshot on a cheater that keeps you coming back. Maybe it’s masochism. Maybe it’s nostalgia. Or maybe it’s the tiny sliver of hope that one day, your team will actually know how to press “W” and hold an angle. A gamer can dream, right?

In conclusion...

Counter-Strike 2 is like a toxic relationship with a twist of Stockholm Syndrome. It’s infuriating, hilarious, and utterly addictive. It’s the kind of game where you’ll spend an entire weekend losing, only to have one amazing round that makes it all worthwhile. You’ll meet people who are absolute legends and others who genuinely seem like they’ve never seen a computer before. You’ll encounter language barriers, cheaters, slow reflexes, and arguments over whether to rush A or B that sound like political debates.

And yet, for some reason, you’ll keep queuing up for another game. Because when it all comes together, when your team actually communicates, when your shots land, and when you pull off a crazy clutch play—it’s the best damn feeling in the world.

So yeah, 10/10 game. Would lose my hairline again.

Before the CS2 release, this was the best shooter available hands down. Could run on a potato, the ranking system made sense and it was fun with many different game modes. Unfortunately Valve has made sure that the game is on its way to the trash. I will point you towards many reasons as to why this game is going to die in a dumpster fire in the next years. 

-Performance
This is the main issue with the game, that plagues every single player no matter the PC. FPS is inconsistent, with even the high-end PCs struggling to maintain stable FPS. An example was a recent teammate - we were playing Premier (i'll touch on this later), and he was complaining that with a RTX 4080, he was getting anywhere from 70-300 FPS. If you know anything about CS in general, it is that you need as many frames as you can get, so this is far from optimal. Random crashes, random disconnects, random freezes when you start shooting or meet an enemy. Play the game for one hour and you will have teammates who have these problems. Pretty sad.

-Skins
This is a blessing and a curse at the same time for the game. CS2 has skins that you can get from loot boxes (cases), which is essentially gambling in its purest form. Another way of getting skins is through the Steam market, but the prices are inflated so much, due to the fact that Valve taxes you on every purchase and sale. So selling these items on the Steam market makes no sense, you have to use 3rd party websites.

-Premier
The old ranked system as it was in CS:GO made sense and created memes. Imagine a game being so good, that its ranking system creates an internet subculture. With the release of CS2 they said to hell with it, we are making an ELO system, so the already toxic community becomes twice as toxic with every loss. Not only that, but the matchmaking makes absolutely zero sense, you are not matched up with players based on your ELO rating, you are being matched up with others based on another hidden rating, that no one has any idea about.

text:
[h1]Counter-Strike 2: Evolution or Revolution?[/h1]

Hey CS fans! I've been grinding Counter-Strike for about 3 years now, cutting my teeth on CS:GO. When CS2 dropped, I was hyped but nervous. Would my hard-earned skills transfer? Would it still feel like the game I've poured countless hours into? After giving CS2 a solid run, here's my take.

[h2]The Source 2 Glow-Up[/h2]

First things first - this game is PRETTY. Coming from CS:GO, the visual upgrade is no joke:

[list]
[*]The lighting is insane. Dust 2 actually looks like a sun-baked desert now!
[*]Character models are crisp. No more squinting to spot enemies.
[*]Smoother performance. My mid-range PC is loving life.
[/list]

But it's not just about looks. The Source 2 engine brings some gameplay changes that took some getting used to:

[list]
[*]Smokes are wild now. They billow realistically and interact with the environment. Took me a while to adapt my strats.
[*]Hit registration feels more consistent. Less "How did that not hit?!" moments.
[*]Movement is subtly different. It's smoother, but it threw off my muscle memory for a bit.
[/list]

[h2]Gameplay: Familiar Yet Fresh[/h2]

At its core, CS2 still plays like the Counter-Strike I know and love. But there are tweaks:

[list]
[*]Gunplay feels more responsive. Sprays are a bit easier to control (or maybe I'm just improving?).
[*]The economy changes are subtle but impactful. Had to rethink some of my buy strategies.
[*]Utility usage is more important than ever with the new smoke mechanics.
[/list]

[h2]Maps: Old Friends, New Looks[/h2]

The classic maps are back, but they've had more than a facelift:

[list]
[*]Visibility is way better. No more dark corners to hide in (RIP my sneaky plays).
[*]Some subtle layout changes. My old nade lineups needed tweaking.
[*]The attention to detail is crazy. I'm still noticing new things.
[/list]

[h2]The Learning Curve[/h2]

As someone who's invested a lot of time in CS:GO, the transition had its ups and downs:

[list]
[*]My aim translated well, but I had to relearn some spray patterns.
[*]Utility usage required practice. Those new smoke dynamics are game-changing.
[*]The pace feels slightly faster, which I'm loving.
[/list]

[h2]Community Vibes[/h2]

The CS community is as lively as ever:

[list]
[*]Matchmaking seems a bit better, but team balance can still be hit or miss.
[*]Lots of returning players, which is cool to see.
[*]The cheating situation feels... about the same. Some matches are still frustrating.
[/list]

[h2]My Verdict[/h2]

As someone who's been with CS:GO for a few years, CS2 feels like a natural evolution. It's familiar enough that I didn't feel lost, but fresh enough to reignite my enthusiasm for the game.

Is it perfect? Nah. There are still bugs to squash and balance issues to iron out. But the foundation is solid, and I'm excited to see where it goes from here.

If you're a CS:GO player on the fence, I'd say dive in. Your skills will transfer, and the new elements add some spice to the gameplay we know and love.

And if you're new to Counter-Strike? Well, you picked a hell of a time to join. The game's looking better than ever, and the core gameplay is still as addictive as always.

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]

CS2 feels like Counter-Strike growing up. It's taken what made CS:GO great and polished it to a shine. As someone who's spent the last 3 years climbing the ranks in CS:GO, I can say that CS2 has successfully rekindled my passion for the game.

Sure, there's a learning curve, especially with the new smoke mechanics and subtle changes to the maps. But that's part of the fun, right? Learning, adapting, and eventually mastering these new elements.

Whether you're a veteran like me or a complete newcomer, CS2 offers something fresh while keeping the core of what makes Counter-Strike great. Now, if you'll excuse me, I've got some new smoke lineups to learn!

[hr]

[i]This review is based on my transition from 3 years of CS:GO to CS2, as of late 2024. The game's still evolving, so who knows what new surprises Valve has in store for us![/i]

Mic istoric Counter-Strike
M-am apucat de Counter Strike inca de cand a aparut aprox. 99".
Cand eram mic am jucat in sala din bloc alaturi de prieteni pana in anul 2005 cand parintii mi-au achizitionat un PC, atunci mi-am facut si primul cont de steam (care din pacate a fost furat > copil > naiv > the end).

De cand joc CS:GO?
Joc CS:GO de cand au aparut skill grupurile (rank-urile) din iarna anului 2012. Pana sa bage operatiunea Payback implicit skin-urile pe arme nu am jucat aproape deloc intrucat jocul mi se parea foarte prost optimizat.

Am inceput sa ma joc alaturi de Administratia Indungi (TucsoN / iBen), ei m-au si indemnat sa imi cumpar prima operatiune Payback insa atunci nu concepeam ideea de a baga bani intr-un joc virtual (nu o percep nici in momentul de fata).

Jocul a inceput sa imi placa de cand s-a bagat a doua operatiunea Pheonix dar in conditiile in care aveam un calculator destul de slab ma jucam doar mapa Nuke si atingeam "performanta" de 30/40 FPS-uri.

Am jucat doar aceasta mapa pana cand am invatat pozitiile. FPS-ul in joc nu ma ajuta foarte mult.. cand eram 1vs1 cu M4A4 / Ak47 imi frama jocul si nu aveam atat de multe sanse sa il iau pe inamic asadar am inceput sa joc cu P90 ascultand de sfatul prietenilor.

A doua operatiune "BRAVO" am cumparat-o deoarece aveai mai multe sanse de drop a armelor / cutiilor plus facilitatile oferite de aceasta. Dupa care a inceput sa imi placa acea iconita pe care ti-o da automat la cumpararea operatiunii si am inceput sa colectionez fiecare badge/iconita/operatiune. De ce mi-a placut ideea? Pentru ca iti contorizeaza toate meciurile/mvp-urile pe langa facilitatile oferite de operatiunea in sine in care iti ofera o poarta de dezvoltare pe plan financiar. Asadar de aici au inceput trade-urile.

Din ce am facut itemele?
In acea perioada aveam un server de SA:MP si acesta m-a ajutat foarte mult pe planul itemelor deoarece v-am spus mai sus.. eu nu sunt de acord sa bagi bani intr-un joc virtual, asadar am inceput sa imi iau cateva iteme de tip (awp boom / glock fade / ak-47 fireserpent / m4a4 howl / awp si m4a4 asiimov / karambit si bayoneta crimson web si multe altele. totul fiind achizitionat din profitul serverului de SA:MP.

Ce am facut cu acestea?
Am hotarat dupa o buna perioada de timp ca nu are rost sa tin ~1500 euro in inventar si sa ma joc in 40 de FPS-uri asadar mi-am vandut toate itemele pentru bani reali si asa am investit in PC-ul si in perifericele pe care le-am folosit o lunga durata de timp > http://www.pcgarage.ro/vizualizare-wishlist/1097152/

Ce intentii am in acest joc?
De fel nu imi place sa pierd asadar vreau sa castig fiecare meci. Din cauza asta nu joc cu oricine.
Voi colecta toate operatiunile si voi incerca sa le fac GOLD (mai putin cea Payback pe care nu am apucat sa o fac datorita celor spuse mai sus).
Rank-ul nu ma intereseaza insa incerc sa il mentin ridicat.
Inca nu ma consider un jucator bun asadar exersez zilnic si ma antrenez pe servere de FFA / arena 1vs1 / si mapele de aim din workshop.
Ce tine de itemele din inventar le tin / cumpar strict doar pe cele care imi plac (gusturile nu se discuta).

Ce sfat ofer altor oameni care citesc acest review?
1. Jocul este placut daca ai un calculator care iti duce peste 100/150 FPS-uri in caz contrar nu ai de ce sa te apuci de joc pentru ca te vei enerva, nu vei sti sa tragi / nu vei face niciodata o performanta in joc.
2. Nu iti lua "painea de la gura", alocatia, banii lu' ma-ta ca sa iti cumperi arme/operatiuni etc.
3. Fii foarte precaut daca ai iteme deoarece esti prada "scammerilor / tepuitorilor".
4. Jocul e placut pana cand dai de codati. Asadar daca dai de codati te vei enerva > apare tentatia de a-ti cumpara cod > primesti VAC BAN > iti pierzi contul de steam si banii investiti in el > iti arunci calculatorul pe geam si te bate si ma-ta so.. calm down pentru cei care vor sa isi cumpere coduri.
5. Antreneaza-te pe servere de FFA (free for all) / Arena (1vs1 /aim map) si joaca mult timp cu boti pentru a invata sa faci SPRAY CONTROL > like pashabiceps.
6. NU juca niciodata singur.. oamenii te vor trage in jos si ca sa fii tu "carry on" si sa ii cari pe toti e greu, sfatul meu > fa-ti o echipa de 5 (+o rezerva).

Acestea fiind spuse tin sa iti multumesc daca ai citit acest review si sper sa va fi ajutat!

text:
Playing CS is what happens when you throw a bunch of heavily armed soldiers into a tiny map and expect strategy. It's like signing up for an emotional rollercoaster designed by a team of trolls with a deep love for random physics and unpredictable teammates

First of all, the game is pretty simple: just aim, shoot, and win, right? WRONG. Bullets in CS
have their own agenda. You can be aiming perfectly at someone's head, standing still, taking a deep breath like you're about to shoot a perfect Olympic gold medal shot... and then somehow, your bullet flies past them. Sometimes I wonder if my crosshair is allergic to enemy heads.

Then there’s the economy system. You buy a gun, do absolutely nothing useful with it for the entire round, die immediately, and end up broke in the next round. Meanwhile, the guy who hasn't bought a gun in three rounds pulls out an AWP like he’s got Elon Musk money. I once had to play with a pistol so many rounds in a row that I started to develop a deep emotional bond with my default Glock. I even named it.

Teammates are a special breed of entertainment in CS
. You’ve got the tactical mastermind, constantly shouting military orders over the mic like we're infiltrating a real-life terrorist camp. You’ve got the guy who thinks he’s in The Matrix, trying to dodge bullets by crouch-spamming in a corner. And then there’s the guy who just discovered the chat wheel and won't stop spamming "Rush B!" every 5 seconds, even when we're on defense. My personal favourite is the "I accidentally bought a sniper but I don't know how to use it" guy, who ends up using the AWP like a shotgun and wondering why things didn’t go well.

Let’s talk about the maps, or rather THE map. Dust II has seen more gunfights than any area in the middle east, yet it remains everyone's favorite place to die. It’s like an ancient artifact at this point.

But despite all the chaos, random headshots, and the occasional rage-quit after being one-tapped by a guy named xXx_SniperLord420_xXx, CS is an absolute blast. There’s nothing quite like the thrill of a 1v5 clutch where you know you're about to make history… only to throw a flashbang at your own feet and blind yourself into oblivion.

In conclusion, CS is the game that will teach you one thing for sure: how to fail with style. But hey, it’s a team effort… or at least that’s what I tell myself when I finish with two kills and 14 deaths.

Verdict: 10/10 would get one-tapped through a wall again.

Counter-Strike 2 is a triumphant return for one of the most iconic first-person shooters in gaming history. Building on the strong foundation of its predecessor, Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS

The first thing you'll notice is the visual overhaul. Powered by the Source 2 engine, Counter-Strike 2 delivers stunning, crisp graphics without sacrificing the fast-paced action the series is known for. Maps like Dust2, Inferno, and Mirage have been given a fresh coat of paint, with improved lighting, textures, and environmental details that make every corner feel more immersive. The changes don’t just look good—they also improve visibility and strategic clarity, making each match feel more dynamic.

In terms of gameplay, Counter-Strike 2 stays true to its roots, but with refined mechanics that make the experience smoother and more responsive. The gunplay is as tight and rewarding as ever, with each weapon feeling distinct and balanced. Movement feels slightly more polished, and subtle tweaks to the physics make engagements feel even more precise. New and updated smoke grenade mechanics, such as volumetric smoke that reacts to bullets and explosions, add fresh layers of strategy to matches, allowing players to manipulate the battlefield in new ways.

Competitive play remains the heart of Counter-Strike 2, and the game offers plenty of features for both casual and hardcore players. Ranked matchmaking is as intense as ever, with a ranking system that rewards skill, communication, and teamwork. Valve has also put more emphasis on anti-cheat measures, making the competitive experience fairer and more enjoyable for everyone.

One of the most impressive aspects of Counter-Strike 2 is how it balances nostalgia with innovation. Longtime fans will appreciate that the core gameplay hasn’t changed drastically—it's still the skill-based, high-stakes tactical shooter that requires sharp reflexes and strategic thinking. Yet, the game also feels refreshed with subtle enhancements, ensuring it stays relevant in today’s FPS landscape.

Overall, Counter-Strike 2 is a fantastic evolution of a classic. It successfully modernizes the beloved franchise while staying true to what made it a legend in competitive gaming. Whether you're a veteran of the series or a newcomer, this game offers a thrilling, tactical experience that will keep you coming back for more. Valve has delivered a sequel worthy of its legacy, making Counter-Strike 2 a must-play for any FPS fan.

text:
With over 10 years and 3,000 hours playing Counter Strike, I would not advise investing into this game.  It is inaccurate to combine the positive ratings from CS:GO with recent ratings of CS2, as these steam reviews currently are.  Since the launch of CS2, we have taken several steps backwards which all together incrementally add up to a subpar experience with no line of sight to resolution.

When moving to CS2, we have lost game modes (i.e Danger Zone), while others have become BOT farming centers not viable for actual play (i.e Casual). Community server game modes do not work as they did in GO (KZ - Movement inconsistencies remain, Surf - Player models clip into edges and dont travel properly).  Valve has not addressed these concerns a year into this new iteration.

It would be unfair to note the issue of cheating and the inability for VAC to curb them.  As much as an issue this remains, it existed in GO and will likely always exist in competitive FPS games.  What is unfortunate is that the most competitive gamemode supported by the developer, Premier, has these problems while other competitor games offer more intrusive anti-cheat solutions for those that desire the competitive experience.  For this reason, third party vendors like FACEIT remain the best place for proper competitive play.  

In CSGO, these third party companies also hosted better servers with better response times (128 vs 64 tick).  However, in CS2, support for 128 tick was entirely removed as develops do not want to support it.  At face value, understandable, developers choice.  However, after a year of development on CS2, Valve remains unable to meet the expectations of the player base on game and server quality.  Many players were patient, understanding the development for GO took a long time get right.  Some remain patient, but we still have no line of sight to resolution timelines.

Moreover, recent updates have had a significantly negative impact on performance.  FPS drops and networking issues make the game less enjoyable.  Many people smarter than me can properly explain the reasons for this, but i shouldn't need a degree in computer science and a deep understanding of networking and all the technical settings within the game in order to be able to play properly.  Developers and/or other community members attributing these issues to poor internet is unfair when these issues didn't exist before the update, in GO, or currently in any other competitive FPS game.

The straw that breaks the camels back - Valve has also taken a further step to over-monetize CS2.  I have been of the belief for some time that Valve has put more emphasis on the skin economy and collectable cosmetics than the quality of the game which brought value to these cosmetics in the first place, but it comes as a slap in the face to take extra steps to earn more while not only failing to address game quality issues, but by actively doing changes to decrease performance and make the experience less enjoyable.

For these reasons, CS2 is not a game i can justify putting my time into any further,  Any cosmetics of value i had were sold off, and my time and attention will be moving to other games.  

TLDR:  Since the release of CS2, the game hasnt been brought back to the standards set by Go.  Updates decrease performance and make the game not fun.  Valve has taken their already predatory monetization approach a step further instead of focusing on game issues.  Do not recommend at this time.

[h1]Pachinko for Children: Welcome to the Glittering World of Arcade Economics![/h1]

[b]What's the deal here?[/b] At first glance, you might think "Pachinko for Children" is an innocent game meant to recreate the colorful chaos of a Japanese arcade. But don't let the cute pixels fool you—this game is essentially a crash course in Economics 101, courtesy of our pals at Valve.

[h2]Valve's Non-Master Plan: The Art of Doing Precisely Nothing[/h2]

[list]
    [*][b]ID Verification Wonderland:[/b] Here's a fun idea—what if Valve implemented a system where your game ban expires only when your ID does? It's a brilliant concept that could change the face of online gaming accountability. And yet, Valve seems more interested in collecting skins than enforcing bans with real-world teeth.
    [*][b]Big Brother's Drive Scanning:[/b] A perfect opportunity for Valve to step into the shoes of a digital overseer, ensuring cheaters can't hide. But will they implement such a system? Seems like they prefer to maintain a 'see no evil' approach, unless it involves transaction errors in their favor.
    [*][b]Tick Issues and Gameplay Glitches:[/b] These could be resolved, transforming gameplay into a seamless experience. But alas, Valve appears to find a strange comfort in the familiar chaos of unresolved issues. Why fix what can mysteriously generate more forum posts?
[/list]

[h3]Nostalgia Isn't What It Used to Be[/h3]

Remember the good old days of CS 1.6, Source, and Global Offensive? This game makes you miss those days like you miss not paying bills. The charm of the original games is still there, buried under a pile of modern-day gambling mechanics.

[b]My Friends' Annual Pilgrimage:[/b] I've seen friends leave the game faster than a cat in a bathtub. They only return once a year, drawn by nostalgia or the urge to check if their digital weapon skins have become the Beanie Babies of the gaming world.

[h3]The Emotional Rollercoaster of Playing "Pachinko for Children"[/h3]

[i]Regulation might be coming:[/i] If gaming regulations tighten up, watch Valve scramble like a contestant in a reality show where the prize is keeping your business alive. Until then, the current state of unchecked gambling mechanics makes the game about as enjoyable as finding out your WiFi isn't working.

[b]To Play or Not to Play?[/b] Occasionally, the urge to dive back into this glittering arcade arises, but then I remember the headache of setting up, queuing, and dealing with cheaters—like preparing for date night with my girlfriend only to find out she's left me.

If Riot ever launches a spinoff that skips the sorcery and focuses on raw, spell-free gameplay, expect a mass exodus. Until then, "Pachinko for Children" remains a sparkling, frustrating reminder of what could have been—a game as much about strategy and skill as it is about the luck of the draw (or the roll of the virtual pachinko ball).

text:
Counter-Strike 2 is a triumphant evolution of a legendary franchise, delivering a refined and exhilarating experience that sets the gold standard for competitive FPS gaming. The game stays true to its roots by focusing on pure skill and tactical depth, a stark contrast to modern titles like Valorant that often rely on flashy abilities and hero mechanics. In CS2, every round is a test of precision and strategy, where victories feel earned and deeply rewarding.

The revamped Source 2 engine elevates the experience with smoother gunplay, dynamic lighting, and stunning visuals. Innovations like the new volumetric smoke grenades, which respond to gunfire and explosions, add a fresh layer of strategy to matches. The updated maps are both visually striking and competitively balanced, ensuring that every angle and chokepoint serves a purpose. CS2 maintains its signature intensity while seamlessly integrating these upgrades, making old strategies feel exciting and new.

Another standout feature of CS2 is its accessibility paired with depth. While the learning curve is steep, it’s not insurmountable, and players are rewarded with a sense of progression that’s rare in modern shooters. Unlike games like Call of Duty, which often lean heavily on chaotic spectacle, CS2 keeps its focus sharp and deliberate, rewarding players for skill and mental acuity over randomness or overpowered mechanics.

That said, the game isn’t without its challenges. Cheaters continue to be a frustration for the community, despite Valve’s improvements to its anti-cheat systems. However, these moments are the exception rather than the rule. Most matches showcase the game’s brilliance, filled with clutch plays, perfectly executed strategies, and heart-stopping action. Valve’s track record of continuous improvement gives hope that this issue will become even less significant over time.

Ultimately, Counter-Strike 2 is a masterpiece of competitive gaming, combining razor-sharp mechanics, strategic depth, and an unmatched sense of intensity. While other FPS games like Valorant or Call of Duty cater to broader audiences with more casual elements, CS2 offers a raw and focused experience that rewards dedication and mastery. For players seeking the ultimate test of skill and strategy, there’s no better game on the market.

text:
Valve simply does not care about Counter Strike (and Team Fortress) anymore & refuses to listen to the community. 

When Valve decides to update this game once every century, it's either A) A one or two line bug fix or B) A soulless corporate cash grab (muh skins). There have been ZERO serious updates to this game in it's first year on the market.

Gone are the days of Operation Payback, Bravo, and Phoenix, in which, shortly after the game's release, Valve rewarded community mapmakers with large amounts of exposure and money. 

Gone are Steam Achievements entirely. All of your hard work from CSGO is now gone in an instant. 

Gone is a functional, working community server browser that doesn't Alt+Tab you out of the game. The community server browser has been a staple of Counter Strike since it's freaking beta in 1999.

Gone are Train, Cobblestone, Cache, Season, Tuscan, and many more fan-favorite maps from the competitive mappool.

The movement speed in the game is way too high (See Counter Strike 1.6 or Valorant for how to do movement correctly). Most of the "skill" in this game revolves around hugging a wall, pre-aiming, and running full speed with A or D and getting a cheap frag with peeker's advantage.  It's way more focused on movement than actual shooting. And unlike Quake, Unreal Tournament, or Counter Strike Source (games with fast movement that are actually fun), CS2 just feels depressing to play, even when winning. 

The game still has a massive cheating problem, with it negatively impacting the top levels of Premier Matchmaking. Also, shoutout to Valve for splintering the community even further by separating people queing Premier (essentially old MM) and Competitive MM (which is further splintered into a per map selection for some god awful reason).

I'm not going to go into subtick, because I simply don't know enough about that specific area. All I can say, is that from my perspective, it feels like Valve made this change to shut up the people who wanted 128 Tick competitive servers during CSGO's lifespan. 

I would love to be made wrong, either by the community or Valve (via a serious update) to all of the points of criticism I have levied. However, I sincerely doubt anything substantial will change.

text:
CS2 looks a lot, lot nicer than CS:GO (though someone like myself still prefers old source engine aesthetics..) it makes a lot of sense why valve ported their game, as one of their most profitable titles. However, it amazes me how bad they screwed this up.. Yes, on paper, the games fine - its hitting it's number consistently with it's playercount, profits, and tournament viewership. But actually playing the game sucks. It does.

I'm not exactly good at this game, but I played enough Global Offensive to feel the difference between shots that hit and miss when they shouldn't.. The game is now inherently terrorist sided due to peakers advantage and the beloved ping theory now actually impacting the game. The engine feels sloppy. Although you can definitely tell me that Source 1 is an absolute mess when it comes to coding, no matter the game you play, it feels crisp on the source 1 engine. Only now, last couple weeks, out of the whole year has this game been out that I have enjoyed the movement slightly more, and have the guns felt a bit nicer to shoot. This isn't to say, however, that Source 2 is the major problem here - other games get by fine with this engine, I just think that a shooter like Counter Strike demands sturdier stock. 

A game like Counter-Strike requires pin-point accuracy and perfect playing to win. Counter Strike 2 apparently can not keep up with that at the moment... I will be returning when the game is in a better state. I still enjoy playing this game - getting the occasional ace or just playing (and raging) with friends is still fun, but there is better ways to spend time.. Shots miss when they shouldn't, you can get paired with cheaters and they receive no penalty, while you cannot leave as you lose elo: overall can just be very frustrating putting time into this game. I can go on, but I won't 

This isn't even talking about the lack of updates. What a joke ! 

TL;DR - game is not ready for a full release. Valve continues to show how lazy and incompetent they are at handling their beloved titles with cheater and gameplay problems. Smoke grenades are better than Global Offensive though lol

text:
CS2: A Digital War Crime Disguised as a Video Game (I’d Still Sell My Kidney for a Rank-Up)

This game isn’t just a dumpster fire, it’s the entire landfill, doused in napalm, with a MVP of dashstar* playing in the background. Imagine getting a back-alley lobotomy from a guy named “Dave” who swears the rusty spoon is “vintage aesthetic”. That’s CS2. And you’ll thank him.

The headshots?
Hitboxes were coded by a blindfolded chicken mainlining Red Bull. Your bullets curve like a elementary schoolers cursive while enemies will headshot you through three walls, a 2003 honda civic and the lingering shame of your 7th-grade talent show. Meanwhile, Little Timmy blew all his cash on a Zeus “for the meme” and now hides in a corner humming the Mission Impossible theme.

Teammates: A Tragedy in 3 Acts:

Act 1: They run around the bombsite for 45 seconds eventually they'll get to the window on mirage just to get one-tapped.

Act 2: They scream about your mom’s alleged relationship with a garden gnome.

Act 3: They throw the match… literally. Your time. Your dedication and your sanity. Gone.

Enemies?
The opposing team isn’t just good-they’re Elon Musk’s secret AI project that will finally get him good at video games. They’ll 360-no-scope you before you see them on your screen. And when you lose the round you'll just have enough time to see them T-bag on your body. And after the match, expect them to leave you a trash comment on your profile or a ASCII art of a sw*stika.

Cheaters: The Game’s Unofficial Final Boss
CS2’s servers are less “competitive playground” and more “zoo where the monkeys have access to aimbots.” Every match is a coin flip: either you get a closet cheater pretending they’ve “practiced their spray control” or a gigachad spinbotting so hard their character looks like a Beyblade on espresso. VAC? More like VACation. Valve’s anti-cheat is out here taking naps while dudes named xX_HeadshotJesus_Xx (profile pic: a bowl of corn flakes) with steam account created yesterday and at least 50 -rep comments on their profile teleport behind you. The only thing getting detected here is my will to live, or rather the lack of it.


DEVS: [crickets.mp3]
The last updates are a “fixed a geometry bug on verigo” ahh patches... The community’s begging for important fixes? Nah. They’re too busy adding a skin that makes your glock look like its made out of legos. And the best part? the new skins are not even made by them...

Why Play?
Because misery loves company and this game is the world’s worst group therapy. I’ve lost 87% of my brain cells. My parents can't sleep at night and at this point know every callout in the game and every swear word in my dictionary.

And you know what?
I’ll play tis game again tomorrow.

Final Rating: ★★★☆☆ (It’s so bad it loops back to iconic. Bring popcorn… and a therapist)
