CS 2 is the true successor of CS-GO while also sharing the best things of the outgoing version. The game has only 2 big flaws which made me uninstall it and go back to games like R6-Siege which seems like have a lot more support from the developer.

1. The sub-tick system is a good thing when the servers are actually 128 tick instead of the base 64, basically for the sub tick system to work as intended you need to be playing in FACE-IT otherwise i would argue that the older 64 servers of  CS-GO were getting better hit-reg and less de-sync.

2. I want to clarify that the problem has been gradually coming to light over the year of the Games life. Cheaters in Premier Match Making. There seems to  be no working anti-cheat in CS or a very bad one " might as well turn it off if its there" .The cheater problem has always plagued CS but not to this extent. Reaching 20K Rating in Premier was a real thing up until recently (above 20K there was a 100% guarantee there was at least 1 cheater per team). On the time of writing this review the problem has starting effecting lower Ratings where now its very difficult to reach 20K as there are boosters using cheaters to carry their team to a higher rating. I would argue that there is a 50% chance at least 1 player is a cheater in 10K rating and above. (Keep in mind we are only speaking of the Premier MM) 


PREMIER: What it was and what it is now!

When premier was introduced in CS-GO it was not a paid system or just a badge like now.
To get Premier you didn't have to pay money. You needed to buy CS not premier!
To get Premier status you needed have a 2 factor and a mobile number which would always be assigned to that account. this way less people would risk cheating and getting banned as it was linked to their phone and would not be able to reuse that mobile phone number to make a 2 factor. Then slowly by the years that changed into just being a paid badge that allowed you to play in Premier only MM in ranked and now its just a Badge that shows that you paid to get the game, No 2 factor is needed on new accounts to get the Premier badge as any one cane buy it.

The Premier system is useless and has no future in CS 2. Remove it or make the game cost like CS-GO did before.

Heartbroken by the Cheaters in CS2

Rating: ★★☆☆☆

I’ve been a huge fan of the Counter-Strike series for years, and the release of CS2 was something I looked forward to with immense excitement. The game itself is brilliant—innovative updates, sleek graphics, and the same adrenaline-pumping gameplay that has kept us all hooked. However, there's a critical issue that’s been absolutely heart-breaking for me and many other players: the rampant cheating.

It’s incredibly disheartening to see how many cheaters are ruining the experience. Matches that should be thrilling and competitive often turn into frustrating exercises in futility because of players who use aimbots, wallhacks, and other unfair advantages. It’s not just a rare occurrence; it’s become alarmingly common. For those of us who genuinely enjoy the game and want to compete on a level playing field, it feels like a punch to the gut every time we encounter these cheaters.

I love CS2—it’s a fantastic game with so much potential. But the current state of cheating is so pervasive that it’s overshadowing everything that’s great about the game. The lack of effective anti-cheat measures is making it incredibly difficult to continue playing. It’s reaching a point where I’m seriously considering quitting because, frankly, the enjoyment is being suffocated by the constant presence of cheaters.

Valve, we need a solution. We need robust anti-cheat systems and more active monitoring to protect the integrity of the game. The community is heartbroken, and if things don’t change soon, we might lose more dedicated players like myself. Please address this issue urgently. CS2 deserves better, and so do the players who love it. </3 <3

text:
I had been a long-time fan of Counter-Strike, a game that once defined competitive first-person shooters for me. When Counter-Strike 2 (CS2) was announced, I felt that familiar excitement bubbling up again. The promise of a revamped engine, improved visuals, and the same thrilling tactical gameplay had me counting the days until release. I envisioned long nights with friends, clutch plays, and that adrenaline-fueled rush of a good match.

But the reality? It’s a nightmare.

It didn’t take long after launch for the shine to fade. The first few matches, sure, there were some glimpses of greatness. That familiar feeling was back... until the cheaters showed up. And they kept showing up. And kept showing up.

Every other game was marred by blatant wall hacks, aimbots, and players who seemed to know every move before it happened. It wasn’t subtle either — no, they weren’t even trying to hide it. Some of them would just lock onto heads across the map with pinpoint accuracy, snap-aiming like robots. It quickly became clear that cheating wasn’t just a problem in CS2; it was the problem.

I tried to shrug it off at first. Maybe I was just unlucky with my lobbies, I thought. But match after match, the same issues kept popping up. Soon, it wasn’t just me; everyone in the community started talking about it. Streams, forums, social media — it was filled with frustrated players, all asking the same question: “Why isn’t Valve doing anything?”

The worst part? Valve seemed to be ignoring the issue. Sure, there was the occasional ban wave, but it felt like a drop in the ocean. For every cheater banned, two more took their place. It didn’t feel like a battle Valve was trying to win. They had the tools. VAC (Valve Anti-Cheat) had been around for years, but in CS2, it felt toothless, outdated, completely incapable of handling the epidemic that was tearing the game apart.

I reached a breaking point when I queued into a competitive match and, from round one, a player on the enemy team was blatantly aimbotting. The entire game, this player dominated, ruining any sense of competition. I reported him, but what good did it do? I knew nothing would happen. By the time the game ended, I wasn’t even angry anymore — just numb. I realized then that CS2 wasn’t about skill anymore; it was about who could cheat harder or endure it longer.

Valve’s silence on the matter only made it worse. We got updates about skins, maps, and cosmetics, but not a word on addressing the core problem plaguing the game. It was like watching your favorite sports team crumble while the coach talked about new jerseys instead of fixing the strategy.

I wanted CS2 to succeed. I wanted it to capture that magic that had kept me coming back to the franchise for so many years. But now, it’s just frustrating. A once-great game has been left to rot, with Valve seemingly unwilling to clean up the mess. Until they take a hard stand on cheating, it’s impossible to enjoy the game in any meaningful way.

It’s sad to admit, but as of now, CS2 feels less like a game and more like a playground for cheaters — and Valve is just standing by, watching it burn.

There aren't that many competitve FPS out there that are still open to new players, but while R6 will usually throw you into decent skill-even games at very low elo(though, newcomers game are absolutely stupid there), CS2 is just a complete matchmaking mess and should be thrown out of the window if you're a new FPS player. Even coming from 700h of R6, I have decent aim but some games are just not winnable when each single enemy has more hours than your entire team combined. Comparing Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS) to Counter-Strike 2 (CS2): Evolution or Revolution?

The release of Counter-Strike 2 marks a significant milestone in the Counter-Strike franchise, and for many fans, it raises an important question: How does CS2 stack up against the beloved CS? After all, CS has been the cornerstone of competitive gaming and esports for over a decade. While both games share the same tactical, team-based foundation, CS2 brings some key changes that could shift the experience for old fans and newcomers alike. Let’s break down the evolution from CS to CS2 in terms of graphics, gameplay, mechanics, and overall experience.

Graphics and Performance: A Visual Overhaul One of the most noticeable differences between CS and CS2 is the leap in graphics. While CS was based on the Source engine, CS2 is powered by Valve’s new Source 2 engine, which brings a host of visual upgrades. In CS, maps, models, and effects were functional but often felt dated, especially as technology advanced.

In CS2, everything from the lighting to textures to environmental details has been significantly improved. The maps look sharper and more vibrant, and the enhanced lighting effects bring a more realistic and immersive feel. Characters are more detailed, and there’s a noticeable improvement in how smoke and flashbang effects interact with the environment.

Performance: Despite the better visuals, CS2 manages to maintain excellent performance even on mid-range hardware, thanks to Valve’s optimization of the Source 2 engine. On the other hand, CS could sometimes feel inconsistent with its performance, particularly when it came to lower-end systems, making CS2 a more accessible experience for a wider audience.

Gameplay and Mechanics: Subtle Tweaks, Same Core At its core, CS2 stays true to the tactical, skill-based gameplay that made CS a staple of competitive gaming. The bomb-planting, defusal, and tactical team play are all intact. However, CS2 refines several gameplay mechanics to make the experience feel more fluid.

Movement and Shooting: The movement system in CS was often praised for its responsiveness, but CS2 offers a tighter feel with slightly more responsive controls. The shooting mechanics feel a bit more precise, with improved recoil patterns and smoother weapon handling. The increased emphasis on precision and feedback makes every shot feel more impactful. That said, longtime CS players will still find the transition relatively easy, as it maintains a similar rhythm.

Hit Registration and Netcode: One of the most important changes in CS2 is the updated netcode and hit registration system. In CS, occasional hit registration issues and lag compensation could be frustrating, especially during high-stakes moments. CS2 seems to have addressed many of these issues, offering more consistent hit detection and a better overall feel during intense firefights. This change has a noticeable effect on the competitiveness of the game, as it feels much more "fair" in terms of hitboxes and damage.

Smokes and Utility: CS2 also introduces more advanced mechanics with grenades, particularly with smoke grenades. They behave more realistically, with particles reacting to the environment, adding more depth to utility usage. This means players will need to think even more strategically about how to use smokes, flashes, and molotovs during rounds. While this adds complexity, it also offers a greater range of tactical possibilities, especially for high-level play.

Community Features and Customization: Keeping the Spirit of CS One of the defining characteristics of CS was its thriving community, supported by the Steam Workshop, skins, mods, and community-created maps. CS2 builds on that legacy with even more extensive customization options, as well as support for community-driven content. The ability to create, share, and play custom content is alive and well in CS2, with more tools for both players and creators.

In terms of matchmaking, CS2 introduces a more refined and polished system compared to CS. The new ranked and casual modes feel more streamlined, and Valve’s focus on improving the matchmaking experience seems to result in more balanced and enjoyable matches. While CS had issues with cheaters and smurfing, CS2 incorporates new anti-cheat measures and improved reporting tools, making the experience more secure and fair.

Overall Experience: A Polished Evolution, Not a Revolution
The best way to sum up the transition from CS to CS2 is that it’s an evolution rather than a revolution. The heart of Counter-Strike remains intact—teamwork, skill, strategy—but CS2 has made important tweaks to bring the franchise up to date. The visual improvements, smoother gameplay mechanics, and enhanced tactical depth make CS2 feel like a modernized, more refined version of CS. However, it doesn't stray too far from the formula that made CS the juggernaut it was.

For CS veterans, CS2 offers enough new features and improvements to warrant a return to the game, while newcomers will find an even more polished and visually appealing entry point into the Counter-Strike universe. If you're a fan of the franchise, there’s little reason not to embrace the future of Counter-Strike with CS2.

Verdict:

Graphics & Performance: CS2 offers a visually stunning upgrade while maintaining solid performance across a wide range of systems. Gameplay & Mechanics: CS2 refines CS’s mechanics, with better responsiveness and more tactical depth, particularly with utility usage. Community Features: Both games excel in community-driven content, but CS2 feels more modern and accessible. Overall Experience: CS2 is a polished, evolved version of CS, and while it’s not a revolutionary departure, it builds on the foundation of CS to offer a more refined experience. If you loved CS, you’ll likely fall in love with CS2—it’s the same game you know, but better.

So if you're looking for a pure, unadulterated FPS experience, maybe check back in after they patch… well, everything.

At the moment, this game is a complete dumpster fire.

- No real anti-cheat (which has been literally the most requested fix since the beginning of CS:GO [2012 btw!]). Because of this, not only are cheaters not getting banned, but completely innocent people are instead. Not to mention the fact that the higher levels of Premier are more or less just cheaters in some fashion. - Higher fidelity graphics, which comes as a double-edged sword because a large portion of the community played GO because of it's non-taxing graphics, making it easy to run, and now that community has been completely left out to dry
- Barely any new content, just bug fixes and that's pretty much it. Remember the game is no longer in beta!
- The ranking system in this game is so incredibly bad that third parties have to use their own system, and that system is considered to be more reliable and well respected than the official one. Think of another game that has to do all of this. I can't. Not to mention the fact that these third parties have a more reliable anti-cheat than the game itself.
- As minor as this may be, there are no longer any achievements except one, and that's for launching the game...
- When CS2 was announced, one of the biggest points of excitement was for 128 tick servers. Plenty of other games have this (VAL being the primary example because of it's similarities to CS), and the decision to use sub-tick was such a cop out, sleazy was of fixing the problem, and no one actually thinks sub-tick is a better solution than 128 tick. There is so much money being poured into this game, you cannot say that Valve does not have the means to maintain servers that would provide an objectively better experience for the end user.

This game is fun extremely casually, but don't bother putting an extended amount of time into it, because clearly Valve would rather not put time into it either.

Look, I've been fragging terrorists and defusing bombs since 1.6, so when CS2 dropped, I was skeptical. But damn, Valve's done good this time.

First off, this game is PRETTY. The Source 2 engine is no joke – maps look crisp, lighting is on point, and those new smoke grenades? *chef's kiss* They're not just eye candy; they're game-changers.

Gunplay feels familiar but refined. It's like reuniting with an old friend who's been hitting the gym. Movement is smooth.

But it's not all sunshine and headshots. Launch was a bit of a mess with performance issues. My rig was sweating bullets trying to keep up at first. Also, if you're expecting a ton of new content, you might be disappointed. It's more of a polished CS:GO than a completely new game.

There are still some bugs crawling around, and yeah, I've rage-quit a few times when the game decided to Houdini my bullets. But hey, it's CS – half the fun is complaining about it, right?

Bottom line: If you loved CS:GO, you'll probably love this too. It's free for CS:GO owners, so there's no reason not to give it a shot. Just don't expect it to revolutionize FPS gaming – it's Counter-Strike doing what Counter-Strike does best, just with a fresh coat of paint.

Now if you'll excuse me, I've got some Silver Elites to destroy in Dust II. See you in the server!

[i] Counter-Strike 2 [/i] is a sequel that tries to innovate but stumbles in key areas, making it a frustrating experience for both new and veteran players alike.

The game’s visual updates are a double-edged sword. On one hand, the improved graphics, detailed environments, and new physics add a modern touch to the classic Counter-Strike formula. Smoke grenades that interact with bullets and the environment in a more realistic way are a particularly nice touch. However, these improvements come at a cost. Performance issues, including frame drops and stuttering, are common, even on high-end systems, detracting from the experience, especially in a game where every millisecond counts.

The core gameplay remains familiar, but some of the changes, like weapon rebalancing and tweaks to the economy system, feel unnecessary and disrupt the flow that many players have come to love. Instead of enhancing the experience, these alterations can feel like a step back, making the game less enjoyable for those who have spent years mastering the original mechanics.

Perhaps the most significant issue, though, is the lack of an effective anti-cheat system. Cheating remains rampant, and despite promises of improvements, it’s clear that the current measures aren’t enough. Encountering cheaters in competitive matches is a frequent frustration, and it significantly undermines the integrity of the game. The presence of cheaters, coupled with an anti-cheat system that feels ineffective, makes it difficult to enjoy the competitive aspect of [i] Counter-Strike 2[/i].

In summary, [i] Counter-Strike 2 [/i] offers some improvements but is bogged down by performance issues, controversial gameplay changes, and a persistent cheating problem. While there are moments of enjoyment, the game often feels like a missed opportunity to truly elevate the series. If you’re a fan of the franchise, there’s some fun to be had, but be prepared for a fair share of frustrations along the way.

text:
The game that has single-handedly boosted the global sales of gaming mice and blood pressure medication. If you’ve ever wondered what it’s like to have your reaction time questioned by strangers from across the globe, look no further. CS2 is here to remind you that no matter how good you think you are, there’s always a 12 year-old with 5,000 hours out there who’s better and more than happy to tell you so.

The graphics are like a pair of well-worn sneakers, comfortable, familiar, and slightly scuffed. Sure, they’re not cutting-edge, but who needs lifelike foliage when you can focus on the important things, like getting shot in the face by someone camping behind a dumpster? The gritty textures and realistic lighting make every map feel like a beautiful place to die over and over again.

The community is as warm and welcoming as a Siberian winter. Whether you’re a new player or a grizzled veteran, you’ll be treated to an endless stream of “constructive criticism” from teammates who are convinced they could go pro if it weren’t for all the noobs holding them back.
CS2 is a game of teamwork, unless you’re playing solo, in which case it’s more of a game of “who can blame who the fastest.” Communication is key, which is why every match sounds like a chaotic mix of callouts, complaints, and that one guy playing music through his mic. 

Endless stream of “EZ” after every round, you’ll quickly learn that the true enemy isn’t the other team - it’s your own sanity. But don’t worry, if you can’t handle the heat, there’s always casual mode... where the insults are just as frequent, but slightly less personal. And when it all goes wrong, at least you can take comfort in knowing that it was definitely, 100% someone else’s fault.

Counter-Strike 2 is the ultimate test of patience, skill, and how much abuse you can take before you uninstall it for the third time this week. It’s a game where you’ll experience the highest highs (winning a clutch round) and the lowest lows (losing a clutch round because you were reloading).
Whether you’re chasing the dream of reaching Global Elite or just trying to rank up from Silver, CS2
offers a unique blend of pain and pleasure that’s hard to find anywhere else.

So, prepare for the thrill of victory and the agony of being called a “bot” by someone half your age and to get repeatedly headshot by someone who swears they’re not cheating. Welcome to Counter-Strike 2, where every round is a new opportunity to question your life choices.

text:
Counter-Strike 2 - A Fresh Coat of Paint on a Classic Shooter

Counter-Strike 2 (CS2) has finally landed, and it’s the long-awaited sequel to one of the most iconic first-person shooters of all time. Valve’s reimagining of Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS
) brings updated visuals, refined mechanics, and a few new features to the table. But how does it stack up against its legendary predecessor?

Visual Overhaul and Maps
The most immediately noticeable change in CS2 is the visual upgrade. Built on Valve’s Source 2 engine, the game looks sharper and more detailed than ever before. Maps like Dust2, Inferno, and Mirage have received significant makeovers, with more realistic lighting, textures, and environmental details. These changes enhance the game’s atmosphere without losing the essence of the original maps that players have come to know and love.

However, some players might find the new visuals a bit distracting at first. The added details can make it harder to spot enemies, especially in fast-paced situations. That said, with time, most players will likely adjust to the new look.

Gameplay and Mechanics
At its core, CS2 remains the same tactical shooter that players have been addicted to for decades. The game still rewards precision, strategy, and teamwork, and the gunplay feels as tight and responsive as ever. However, Valve has made some subtle tweaks to the mechanics, such as improved grenade physics and updated sound design, which add depth to the gameplay.

One of the most talked-about additions is the revamped smoke grenade system. Smokes in CS2 are now dynamic, meaning they interact with the environment and other grenades in real time. For example, a grenade blast can momentarily clear a portion of the smoke, creating new opportunities and challenges during a match. This change adds an extra layer of strategy to the game, as players must now think even more carefully about how and when to use their utility.

The Competitive Scene and Community
Counter-Strike has always been a staple in the competitive gaming scene, and CS2 is no different. With its release, we can expect to see a surge of new and returning players eager to climb the ranks. The matchmaking system has been improved, aiming to provide fairer and more balanced matches, although there’s always room for improvement.

The community, as always, is a double-edged sword. On the one hand, the Counter-Strike community is passionate, skilled, and knowledgeable, making for some intense and rewarding matches. On the other hand, like any competitive game, there are moments of toxicity, especially in high-pressure situations. Valve has introduced more tools to combat cheating and toxic behavior, but it remains an ongoing battle.

Performance and Stability
Given its new engine and updated visuals, CS2 generally runs smoothly on modern systems, but older setups might struggle a bit more. Valve has put in a lot of effort to optimize the game, and for the most part, it shows. However, as with any newly released game, there are occasional bugs and performance issues that need to be ironed out. These hiccups aren’t game-breaking but can be annoying, especially in competitive play.

Conclusion
Counter-Strike 2 is a worthy successor to CS
, bringing much-needed visual and mechanical updates to the classic formula. It maintains the core elements that made Counter-Strike a phenomenon while adding enough new features to keep things fresh and exciting. The revamped maps, dynamic smoke grenades, and improved matchmaking system make for a more modern experience without losing the game’s timeless appeal.

However, it’s not without its growing pains. The new visuals might take some getting used to, and performance issues can be a minor hurdle. But for fans of the series, CS2 offers a familiar yet refreshed experience that’s worth diving into.

Rating: 8.5/10

Counter-Strike 2 successfully breathes new life into a classic game, making it a must-play for both veterans and newcomers alike. Just be ready to face some challenges along the way as the community adapts to this new era of Counter-Strike.

I had high hopes for Counter-Strike 2, expecting a refined version of the classic competitive shooter that I've enjoyed for years. Unfortunately, the reality of the game is far from the polished experience I anticipated.

First and foremost, the community is downright toxic. It's almost impossible to play a single match without encountering players who are either throwing insults, harassing others, or engaging in unsportsmanlike behavior. The chat is often flooded with offensive language, and the voice comms are filled with people who seem to get more enjoyment out of belittling their teammates than actually playing the game. It's disheartening to see a game with such potential be dragged down by the very people who play it.

Worse still is the prevalence of cheaters. It feels like every other match is plagued by players using hacks or third-party software to gain an unfair advantage. Whether it's wallhacks, aimbots, or other exploits, the frequency of cheaters has made the game virtually unplayable at times. The in-game reporting system seems ineffective, as these players continue to run rampant, ruining the experience for those of us who want to play fair.

In its current state, CS2 is a frustrating and demoralizing experience. The toxic community and unchecked cheating have turned what should be a thrilling and competitive game into a cesspool of negativity and unfair play. Unless these issues are addressed, it's hard to recommend this game to anyone. Save yourself the frustration and look elsewhere for your gaming fix.

text:
I still play the game often and I like it, but I leave a negative review because I don't like the direction it's taken. I want CS to become better, I love playing it with my friends, I like the skins, and the community has brought me many laughs, but it feels like Valve is putting the bare minimum effort to keep the game alive and have people spend money. Here's why:

-Game released bare-bones missing many maps and game modes from CSGO

-To date, every new update makes it run worse, the latest update has issues with huge frame drops, stutters, and freezing. Frame in CSGO was consistent 400, now I'm lucky to get 160fps with half decent frame times.

-Community servers are a shambling corpse of what it was in CSGO. That side of the community is dead. All the servers are full of bots. No good AWP only servers, a few good 1v1 servers, no zombies, no deathrun or the other dozens of other fun game mode servers. That whole creative side of the community has been abandoned by Valve and given little support. Surf zoomer are eating well, at least. 

-Maps are pretty BUT the amount of visual clutter only lowers frames and makes it harder to see enemies.

-Ruined factory new skins by giving them all wear. Now a factory new skin looks like a minimal wear or even field tested from CSGO. Example, Bizon Osiris. (thanks for making those skins slightly cheaper, at least)

-Player models are not accurate to hit boxes, the default CT is terrible. I've flicked to parts of the model that don't count as a hit. That is a terrible decision for a competitive game.

-No more default player models that vary depending on the map. Not a big loss, but it shows a lack of attention imo.

-The HUD keeps getting worse. It's amazing how badly they can mess this up. CSGO had a minimalist, clean, and easy to read HUD with all the important info in places that have a physical reference point irl, like the health at the bottom left. New CS2 HUD has transparency on everything, selected items don't highlight as well, I really miss the nice touch of my weapons being highlighted in the color of their rarity, mini map is harder to read, my money is bigger than my health or armor, and I don't need to know what team I am by having a big emblem in the middle of my screen. The HUD is provably and quantifiably worse than in CSGO.

-Why do we have first shot inaccuracy?? Why? Makes zero sense in this type of competitive game. Why do I need to miss my one-tap headshot when my aim is on the enemy's head? Is the game really better for having that?

-Hacker issue still not fix, and the hacks have only gotten more powerful. We are talking Rainbow Six Siege levels of absurd hacks. They can change the spread of shotguns and change the the fire rate, absurd things like that.

-Ranks and elo systems are terrible and matchmaking will put you in games that will force you to lose. I'm talking about putting you against teams with 5k more elo than anyone on your team.

-Still no overwatch system like in CSGO.

-The biggest updates we got until now is a few community maps and the ability to switch hand view model... SIX months in. You know the community is starving for content when that is considered a huge update. In CSGO that would be a normal bi-monthly update.

-Hit reg is terrible and it's probably sub-tick being terrible. 

-AWP nerfs were not needed and makes it frustrating to use. Inaccuracy when getting hit is terrible and taking longer for the scope to settle after aiming makes getting quick kills a game of luck at times. text:
Counter-Strike 2 is a popular first-person shooter (FPS) game developed by Valve Corporation and Hidden Path Entertainment. Initially released in 2012, CS:GO quickly gained a massive player base and became a staple in the competitive gaming scene. With its intense gameplay, strategic depth, and dedicated community, CS:GO has remained a prominent title in the FPS genre for nearly a decade. In this review, we will delve into the various aspects of CS2, the sequel, highlighting its strengths and weaknesses.

Positive Aspects:

1. Tactical Gameplay:
CS2 is renowned for its strategic depth and tactical gameplay. Success in this game requires not just sharp reflexes but also solid teamwork, communication, and decision-making. The emphasis on strategy makes every match feel like a mental chess game, where players must outsmart their opponents through clever positioning, weapon choices, and map knowledge.

2. Skill-Based Gameplay:
One of the key strengths of CS2 is its high skill ceiling. Mastering the game requires honing various skills such as aiming, recoil control, movement, and game sense. The satisfaction of landing precise headshots, executing clutch plays, and outmaneuvering opponents through sheer skill is unmatched and keeps players coming back for more.

3. Competitive Scene:
CS2 boasts a vibrant competitive scene with regular tournaments, leagues, and a robust ranking system. The game's emphasis on fair gameplay and skill-based matchmaking ensures that matches are both challenging and rewarding. The thrill of climbing the ranks and competing against top players adds an exciting dimension to the game.

4. Weapon Variety and Customization:
CS2 offers a wide array of weapons with distinct characteristics, allowing players to find their preferred playstyle. From rifles and pistols to grenades and sniper rifles, the game provides ample choices for players to experiment with. Additionally, the ability to customize weapon skins and stickers adds a personal touch to the gameplay experience.

5. Active Community and Updates:
The CS2 community is known for its passion and dedication to the game. Valve's continuous support through updates, bug fixes, and new content keeps the player base engaged and invested in the game. Community-created maps, skins, and game modes further enrich the gameplay experience and contribute to the game's longevity.

Negative Aspects:

1. Cheating and Toxicity:
One of the major drawbacks of CS2 is the prevalence of cheaters and toxic behavior in the community. Hackers using aimbots and wallhacks can severely impact the competitive integrity of matches, leading to frustration among legitimate players. Additionally, toxic behavior, trolling, and verbal abuse can create a hostile environment that detracts from the overall gaming experience.

2. Outdated Graphics:
Despite its strong gameplay mechanics, CS2's graphics engine shows signs of aging. The visuals, while functional, lack the polish and detail seen in newer FPS titles. Players accustomed to modern graphics may find CS2's visuals underwhelming, particularly in comparison to more graphically demanding games on the market.

3. Limited Innovation:
Over the years, CS2 has received incremental updates and additions without introducing significant innovations to the core gameplay. While the game's formula has proven to be successful, some players may crave fresh mechanics, features, or game modes to breathe new life into the experience. The lack of substantial innovation could lead to stagnation for long-time players.

4. Hit Registration and Netcode Issues:
CS2 has been criticized for occasional hit registration issues and inconsistencies in its netcode. Players may experience instances where shots that appear to be on target do not register, leading to frustrating outcomes. Addressing these technical issues and improving the game's netcode could enhance the overall gameplay experience for all players.

Conclusion:
CS2 remains a standout title in the FPS genre, thanks to its tactical depth, skill-based gameplay, and competitive nature. The game's dedicated community, frequent updates, and engaging gameplay contribute to its enduring popularity. While CS2 has its share of shortcomings, such as cheating problems and outdated graphics, its strengths far outweigh its weaknesses. Whether you're a seasoned veteran or a newcomer to the series, CS2 offers a challenging and rewarding experience that is worth exploring.

Final Verdict: 9/10

This chaos not only makes the game less enjoyable but also destroys the competitive balance that should be the cornerstone of any high-level gaming experience.

The prevalence of cheaters leads to significant rank inflation and deflation. Honest players find their ranks either artificially inflated by being on teams with cheaters or deflated by constantly losing to cheaters. Widespread cheating has created a toxic community atmosphere. Suspicion and false accusations run rampant, eroding trust among players. This lack of trust destroys the sense of camaraderie and fair play that should define the gaming community.

While the game developers claim to be combating cheating, their efforts have proven woefully inadequate. The anti-cheat measures in place are ineffective, and cheaters continue to thrive. This failure on the part of the developers is a significant part of why this game remains unplayable for honest players.

In summary, I would not recommend this game to anyone—ever. The cheating problem is so severe and pervasive that it completely undermines the gaming experience. text:
Counter-Strike 2: Global Pandemonium (not really its name, but it should be) is the adrenaline-fueled offspring of a tactical shooter and a comedy sketch. It drops you into a world where terrorists and counter-terrorists battle it out in scenarios that range from defusing bombs to rescuing hostages—because apparently, both sides have a lot of spare time between rounds to debate who has the better facial hair.

Graphically, it's a bit like peering through a pair of binoculars smeared with peanut butter, but hey, that just adds to the challenge, right? You'll squint through murky hallways and dimly lit bomb sites, praying that the blob in the distance isn't your teammate about to accidentally spray you with an AK-47. And let's not forget the character models—somehow, they manage to look simultaneously like hardened special forces operatives and rejected extras from a B-movie set in a back alley.

Gameplay is where the hilarity really kicks in. You'll spend minutes planning your strategy with military precision, only for it to fall apart faster than a house of cards in a hurricane. Rushing in with a knife? Sure, why not. Trying to snipe from across the map with a pistol? Go for it, cowboy. It's a symphony of chaos and unpredictability, with each round resembling a game of "Hot Potato" where the bomb is, well, a bomb, and no one wants to be left holding it when the music stops.

Weapons in Counter-Strike 2 are like a dysfunctional family reunion. You've got your classics—the AK-47 that kicks like a mule on roller skates, the AWP that promises one-shot kills if you can hit the broad side of a barn (spoiler: you can't), and of course, the trusty Desert Eagle that makes you feel like an action hero until you miss every shot and get turned into Swiss cheese by a P90-wielding maniac.

Playing with friends turns the hilarity up to eleven. Communication is key, especially when you're trying to coordinate a synchronized rush while simultaneously arguing over who ate the last slice of virtual pizza in the safe zone. Friendly fire incidents? They're not accidents; they're team-building exercises in trust and forgiveness. And let's not forget the post-round banter, where you'll either celebrate victory with triumphant cheers or console each other after yet another humiliating defeat.

But beneath the laughs and the occasional rage-induced keyboard smash, Counter-Strike 2 has a strange allure. It's the thrill of pulling off a clutch play against all odds, the satisfaction of outsmarting your opponents with a well-timed flashbang, and the camaraderie that comes from sharing unforgettable moments—like that time you accidentally defused the bomb with two seconds left because you thought it was a toaster.

Counter-Strike 2: Global Pandemonium is not just a game; it's a comedy of errors, a heart-pounding adrenaline rush, and a testament to the absurdity of virtual warfare. Whether you're a seasoned veteran or a fresh-faced recruit, every round is a chance to laugh, learn, and occasionally question your life choices as you respawn for the umpteenth time. So grab your guns, rally your team, and embrace the chaos—it's time to show those terrorists (or counter-terrorists) who's boss, one hilarious round at a time.

I grew up on Counter-Strike, it's more of what we all like. I will never not own the latest version of this game.

text:
Like most tactical shooters, it takes a bit of time and learning to become a competent player. The learning curve can feel a bit steep if you're new to Counter Strike since many players have years of applicable knowledge from the previous games. At the time of this review, I've played against several obvious cheaters, mostly people with wall hacks in the casual playlist; though I'd expect you come across cheaters in higher competitive and premier ranks. Word of advice, if someone in your lobby accuses another player of cheating, spectate them when you get an opportunity to verify, before vote kicking. Unfortunately, people cry wolf about cheaters frequent enough, it can be difficult to get your teammates to take a cheating accusation seriously or they just don't care their teammates a cheater, because they want to win.

Going back to becoming a competent player. Start out by learning spray patterns of a handful of guns using one of the workshop maps. In addition to that, watch some videos on YouTube about a handful of maps and learn the basics. Probably best to learn maps within the same matchmaking playlist to help focus your learning. With that said, most of the players I've come across have been friendly. Though, be warned, while you're starting out, expect to run into some players who are less than gracious to newer players. Just comes with it being a competitive shooter game, if you've ever played Rainbow Six: Siege, you know what to expect.

Overall, fun game. Doesn’t have as wide of an appeal as Call of Duty, but I'd say give it a shot and try to learn the basics before uninstalling.

text:
Hey hey people, millennial here. I remember Boom Headshot guy and when Youtube *wasn't* owned by Google. And I've played Counter-Strike since, well, Counter-Strike (1.6). It was the only FPS that would run on my potato laptop that I appropriated from my dad (he had enough computers already, all running Windows 98). Anyway, the laptop had a floppy disk drive. That should give you an idea of how old it was. But at least it had Win XP, which booted in 5 minutes instead of 10.

In secondary school, I got a wee lil 1st gen Core i3 laptop on which I immediately got 3 things: Halo CE, CoD4, and CS:S. Later, I got L4D and discovered that its versus mode was objectively more fun than CSS. All we did was play offline with classmates on a LAN cable, so the AI zombies massively increased replayability, which CS didn't have. Alas, I have to say, it's fundamentally a very monotonous game, with its only diversity being in the openings and gambits that each team brings, when it can muster any semblance of coordination. It's actually a lot like chess, but with a lot more incoherent screaming, and people at the grandmaster level are viewed by the general public as being no-life nerds instead of sophisticated geniuses. "Esports", kek!

Ahem. Finally, at uni, I got CS:GO. In the neofeudal sh*tehole that is modern Britain, universities are just about the only places in the country that have fibre optic instead of third-world ADSL, available to you at the low low price of £9000 per year. Anyway, this meant about half my flat of 13 could goof off teamkilling each other at the same time. Brilliant, 10/10, many hours wasted in this way. Overwatch, PUBG and R6: Siege also scratched this itch, being also games where you can largely be an idiot with your mates while chatting shit about whatever.

Now, I haven't touched CS:GO in years (not since 2017, basically), and I'll get to that in a sec. A while back I vaguely heard CS:2 was coming out. Oh cool, I thought, now we have 4 Counter Strikes, but still not more than 2 of any of the good Valve games (Team Fortress, L4D, and Half Life)! But lo and behold, some time later, I happen to look at my Steam Library and see that CS:2 is in fact not a separate game, and has instead gruesomely evolved from the carcass of CS:GO in what can only be described as an artificially-induced nonconsensual digital metamorphosis. Oh, hang on, sorry - I got distracted and started describing Overwatch 2 there! CS:2 is actually okay, it's more of just an overhyped update that changed smokes and basically nothing else. At the end of the day, the game really hasn't become anything new, so I won't be returning to it.

So why do I dislike CS so much for someone with hundreds of hours in it? Well, simply put, it is the League of Legends of shooters. I suppose Valorant fills that role too, but I haven't touched it because I'm allergic to zoomers. The only real difference is that it's an FPS instead of a MOBA, and that CS doesn't have any champions or heroes to select. 

But the core essence of the game in terms of how you will spend your time is identical: it's a sweaty, toxic, and intensely repetitive micro-transaction riddled clown fiesta that teams you up with four other morons so you can yell at each other and accomplish nothing for the better part of the next hour. If you actually hate yourself, you can even queue up for Ranked and multiply these horrors tenfold!

So why did I play it so much? Well, again, just like League of Legends, it's actually really fun if you're just being stupid with your friends. 5-stack Tec-9s and rush down a dumb position and laugh like hyenas when it works (or doesn't). Go all Negev. Go 1 AWP and juggle it while everyone else tries for 1-Deags. Buy nothing but smokes and shotguns. To not take it seriously is the only way to make the game fun; same as PUBG or LoL, really. Also, gun game originated in CS, not CoD, and by god you better put some respect on objectively the best game mode. Many a fun hour were had playing gungame in the undergrad flat. And you better believe I was rocking the shiggydiggy revolver 24/7 during the infamous cowboy update. RIP R8 revolvo, gone too soon, I count 6 shots ni-

Overall, 6.5/10: it's tolerable if you're a full premade. The gunplay is quick and responsive thanks to hitscan and a lack of ADS, and it's very easy to learn the basics. But otherwise, do yourself a favour and play something else, because it's going to be a hard sell for your friends if they aren't already into this kind of game. And for god's sake, don't play it by yourself. I'd tell you to touch grass, but even faceplanting into sandpaper is better than solo queue. Don't do that to yourself, man. 

Anyway, it's a hard decision, but if a game is fundamentally multiplayer-only yet the online experience is awful unless you curate a buffer zone for yourself by dragging friends into your lobby, I think it needs a thumbs-down. By contrast, you can actually have fun with randoms in games like TF2 (at least now that Valve pulled their thumb out for the bot ban wave) and Halo MCC. Of course, if you like the core gunplay and gameplay loop enough, I suppose you can put up with that, but if you already know that about yourself, you probably already have the game and don't really need my review, do you? 

No, this sugandese pseudo-familiar essay is simply meant to deter normies from the sweatfest that is Counter Strike, and encourage a better use of time. There are people with 2000+ hours in this game. I think 200 is already too much. But my name isn't Charles, and I'm not in charge of you. At the end of the day, if you're determined to make a bad decision, you could do worse than Counter-Strike. You could play PUBG, which will waste even more time, be even less rewarding, and also melt your computer!

Blah blah blah so many words. tl;dr: decent game, but its core loop facilitates sweatiness and toxicity a little too well.

text:
CS2 is fun, especially if you have friends (though I wouldn’t know). It’s arguably the best multiplayer tactical shooter out there, with gameplay that’s been top of its class for over two decades. CS2 is a game that requires skill and patience to learn and improve. What keeps this game so fucking popular is its low skill floor but high skill ceiling: the game’s mechanics are simple and consistent, but you’ll never fully master the game, as there’ll always be others better than you, and even reaching a level of ‘kind of good’ takes a [i]lot[/i] of work.

I never played CSGO, which I regret, and this is the first CS game, and even the first tactical shooter, I’ve ever played. I’m far from what I’d consider good, but the game is rarely [i]not[/i] fun.

Now, you may ask, why did I mark this review as not recommended? Well, while I do think CS2 is a great game, it has one humongous, impossible-to-ignore problem: cheaters. CS2 has more cheaters and a worse anti-cheat than literally any other modern shooter out there. VAC hardly does anything, and cheaters are relentless and omnipresent in this game. While it’s fairly rare, but still more common than you’d like, to meet cheaters in lower ranks, they’re everywhere in higher ranks (or so I’ve heard). The old ‘overwatch’ system, a system that’d let any participating player review gameplay demos and decide if a player is cheating or griefing to get them banned or spared, is gone, aside from a few select people with access. VAC is weaker and more useless than any other modern anti-cheat.

Once you have a high enough rank, you’re essentially forced to play FACEIT, a third-party platform and anti-cheat, one that is kernel-level, meaning much stronger (albeit intrusive) than VAC.

What Valve [i][u]really[/u][/i] needs to do is significantly improve Valve Anti-Cheat (and not just for CS2 either). Creating a kernel-level anti-cheat would likely be the best option. Not everyone is a fan of kernel-level anti-cheats, as they essentially have access to your entire system and could significantly fuck your shit up if the company that developed it is shady and malicious. However, it’s seriously unlikely that a company as big as Valve would use their anti-cheat to commit illegal or immoral activities, so that is not a concern in my eyes.

Even if it’s not kernel-level, VAC [i]needs[/i] to be better. Valve has stated that they’re working on an AI-powered anti-cheat, but we’ve not heard any updates about it and have no idea what the ETA on it is. My bet is, it won’t become a thing for at least another two years, if ever.

[hr][/hr]

In conclusion, CS2 is a great game with one major issue that Valve seems to not care that much about. Valve’s terrified of the ‘infinite treadmill’ where they have to keep improving the anti-cheat in order keep cheaters at bay, since cheats will always be improved, so it’s a never-ending battle, just like adblockers vs. the Internet – however, it’s Valve’s responsibility to make sure the game has a functional anti-cheat so it’s fair to everyone. Besides, even just occasionally updating the anti-cheat to bring periodic yet unexpected ban waves would be a significant deterrent for cheaters and would reduce the number of cheaters in this game manyfold.

Counter-Strike 2: A Masterpiece in Competitive Gaming Design

Counter-Strike 2 (CS2) has arrived with a bang, and it’s clear that the developers have not only stayed true to the series’ iconic roots but have also crafted a game that feels remarkably fresh and exhilarating. With a solid combination of nostalgic elements, cutting-edge technology, and innovative design choices, CS2 takes the crown as one of the most well-crafted competitive first-person shooters of this generation.

Visual Overhaul: Beautifully Crafted World

Right off the bat, CS2 impresses with its stunning visual overhaul. Built on the Source 2 engine, the game has a noticeable graphical upgrade while keeping the familiar look that Counter-Strike fans have come to love. The environments are more detailed and immersive than ever, with improved lighting, textures, and particle effects enhancing both the atmosphere and the precision of gameplay. Whether you're carefully peeking around corners or making a last-ditch attempt at securing the bomb site, the visual clarity and smoothness of movement make every action feel intense and fluid.

Sound Design: A Symphony of Strategy

The audio in CS2 is an absolute triumph. The sound design has been meticulously crafted, offering both subtle and explosive moments that are key to gameplay. The directionality of sound is particularly noteworthy—players can now pinpoint enemy positions with unparalleled accuracy, listening for footsteps, gunfire, and grenade bounces that contribute to the strategic depth of the game. These sound cues, paired with the improved voice chat system, ensure that teamwork and communication remain central to the game.

Gameplay: Tight, Responsive, and Deep

CS2 builds on the legendary mechanics of its predecessors while adding subtle refinements that make the game feel tighter and more responsive. Gunplay is as satisfying as ever, with each weapon feeling distinct and impactful. Whether you're spraying bullets with the AK-47 or tapping headshots with a Desert Eagle, the weapon balance has been carefully adjusted, providing a rewarding experience for both casual and competitive players.

The game’s pacing remains brilliant, with classic modes like Bomb Defusal and Hostage Rescue retaining their core appeal. CS2 introduces more intricate tactical possibilities, where teamwork, utility usage, and map knowledge are more important than ever. The introduction of new tools and features, such as updated smokes and flashes, further enriches the tactical landscape, giving experienced players new ways to outsmart their opponents.

Matchmaking & Anti-Cheat: The Competitive Edge

Perhaps one of the most anticipated aspects of CS2 is its matchmaking and anti-cheat systems. Valve has taken massive strides in improving the integrity of the game, ensuring that players of all skill levels can enjoy a fair and balanced experience. The new matchmaking system offers a more dynamic ranking and matchmaking experience that feels rewarding and free of the frustrations of previous iterations. Coupled with an improved anti-cheat system, CS2 has elevated the competitive scene to a level of fairness that’s essential for a game of this caliber.

Community & Esports: A Thriving Ecosystem

One of Counter-Strike’s key strengths has always been its thriving community, and CS2 is no different. The game embraces its roots, fostering a competitive ecosystem while also providing tools for map creators and modders to continue building the world of CS2. The addition of custom skins, maps, and community servers keeps the game feeling alive and fresh, offering a diverse range of experiences for players of all types. The esports scene is as exciting as ever, with CS2 positioning itself as a premier title for both professional players and fans.

Final Verdict: An Unparalleled Experience

Counter-Strike 2 is a triumph of game design. Every aspect, from its visual polish and sound design to its deep, rewarding gameplay, is crafted with love and attention to detail. It strikes the perfect balance between accessibility and depth, ensuring that both new players and seasoned veterans can find something to love. With its flawless competitive mechanics, an evolving community, and stunning technical design, CS2 is poised to be the definitive first-person shooter of this generation. If you’re a fan of tactical shooters, you simply cannot miss this masterpiece.

You can almost hear the collective sigh of the player base every time a cheater slips through the cracks, reminding you that while VAC Live might be watching, it’s definitely not always working.

CS2 offers a thrilling experience where victories are exhilarating, defeats are crushing, and every match is a new chance to blame lag, VAC Live, and your teammates. Dive in, but brace yourself for the wild ride of tactical brilliance and epic frustration.

text:
As a long-time fan of the "Counter-Strike" series, I was eagerly anticipating the release of "Counter-Strike 2." However, after spending considerable time with the game, I have mixed feelings about it. While the graphical enhancements and refined gameplay mechanics are impressive, several critical issues significantly impact my overall experience.

Lack of Effective Anti-Cheat Measures
One of the most glaring shortcomings in "Counter-Strike 2" is the inadequate anti-cheat system. Despite community pleas for robust protections, the game continues to suffer from a rampant cheating problem. The lack of a strong anti-cheat mechanism has allowed cheaters to proliferate, creating an uneven playing field and diminishing the integrity of competitive matches. This issue is a significant deterrent for both new players and veterans, including myself, who often find our enjoyment marred by the presence of unfair play.

Absence of the Overwatch System
In previous iterations, the Overwatch system allowed experienced players to review reported matches and identify cheaters, acting as a supplementary layer of community-driven enforcement. Unfortunately, "Counter-Strike 2" has yet to implement this feature, leaving a void in the game's self-regulatory mechanisms. The absence of Overwatch means that suspicious behavior goes unchecked for longer periods, exacerbating the cheating problem and reducing community trust in the game's fairness.

Horrible Tick Rate Servers
Another major drawback is the poor performance of the game's servers, specifically the low tick rate. In a fast-paced, precision-based game like "Counter-Strike," server tick rate is crucial for ensuring smooth and accurate gameplay. The current low tick rate servers result in inconsistent hit registration and lag, frustrating players like me who expect a seamless competitive experience. This technical issue undermines the core gameplay, leading to widespread dissatisfaction among the player base.

text:
Potential.

That's the only word that really comes to mind immediately with this game. The engine update is a huge deal for detangling decades old spaghetti code CSGO had lingering around because the Source engine was RELEASED in 2004, and it started development years before.

Source 2 is very obviously much more powerful, not just graphically but from a technical perspective it has almost 20 years of R&D both inside and outside of Valve it can draw upon.

But it's not there yet, and it WILL take a while yet.
Valve work at Valve's pace, not ours.
And that pace will cause a lot of present issues drag out for longer than they probably should.
The slightly off movement, the run and gun gameplay being too powerful, the stickiness with teamates making boosts, run boosts and just general movement in tight areas annoying.

And then there's the cheating problem. Valve have recently updated VAC-Live it appears to target blatant spin-botters. And that is FANTASTIC news for those playing premier in higher elo lobbies. But even with those types all but eliminated, the closet cheaters remain, they're more than likely less prevelant than most people claim.
But that DOUBT instilled in peoples brains by this issue seemingly not being dealt with for years both within CSGO and now CS2 causes a lot of players, new and old, to give up playing because they don't know if they lost because someone is walling or radar hacking OR, if they just sucked that game.

You more than likely just sucked that game, but that you can't be sure of that causes doubt that Valve is making any effort to address that issue. The blatant spin botters honestly don't annoy people as much as closet cheaters.
At least with spin botters, you know exactly what the problem is.

I'm hoping the rumors of an AI model being trained for VAC-Live and Overwatch returning are true and help.

But DOUBT, is setting in. And that's the biggest dissapointment of all.

text:
I've long enjoyed this game however CS2 has some pretty major problems which have yet to be resolved. I've held off writing a review since I was hoping by now that it would be in a better state.

[h3] The good [/h3]
I'll start with some things I like. Contrary to how a lot of people feel, I really like the graphical changes. The game is a lot better looking, but still really smooth and consistent (at least in my experience). I also greatly prefer the transparency of having a numerical value for rank as opposed to the categorical ranks of CSGO.

[h3] The bad [/h3]
This game has two major issues though which I think are devastating for the competitive scene.
[b] 1. [/b]
Firstly, elo gain and loss are almost entirely based on team loss/wins with little regard for individual performance. This means that if a GE stacks with 4 silvers continuously, all of their elo will eventually converge to be roughly the same value. I play with people that are much better than me but our elo is almost the same since we play together often. Because of how little information is utilised to adjust your rank, you'd need to solo queue for many matches to get an appropriate elo, which means you end up in an unnecessarily high number of unfair matches (either rolling the enemy team or vice versa). I think Valve tried to remedy this by bootstrapping your initial rank based on individual performance, but the initial number is often way off so this doesn't work. I get the philosophy behind this design, CS is a team based game, but this system doesn't work well in practice.

[b] 2. [/b]
Secondly is the massive overabundance of cheaters and smurfs. The weekly drop system encourages people to make/use alt accounts, causing further problems to matchmaking since you get high rank players in <10k lobbies just trying to earn their drops. Cheating also seems to be a major issue in comparison to CSGO. It seems something has happened to our trust factor, as our match quality has very sharply plummeted and we have lost 11 premier matches (yes, [i] eleven [/i]) in a row, almost all of which had blatant cheaters on the enemy team. Most accounts we play against now are throwaways. Our only hope of winning is to not 5 stack and hope we get a cheater of our own on our team, but that's not fun.

The game just isn't fun anymore since we can't find matches without throwaway cheating accounts, so I plan to take a break from CS2 and just hope that the game ends up in a better state soon so that I can continue playing.

text:
Counter-Strike 2

Gameplay / Content: The core gameplay remains true to the Counter-Strike legacy, offering tight, responsive controls and highly strategic, skill-based combat. New mechanics and refinements, such as improved hit detection and rebalanced weapons add depth. The slight learning curve for newcomers is the only minor drawback, but is an aspect that keeps the game highly competitive. The ranking system is disatisfactory as wins to losses are not balanced (i.e. winning three games and losing two games will decrease your rank significantly). Customization options in Counter-Strike 2 are plentiful, with a wide range of skins, weapon finishes, and player models available. The game supports modding, allowing the community to create custom maps and game modes, adding to its replayability. However, some monetization aspects of customization, such as microtransactions for skins lead many into gambling, as paying money for cases and rolling for skins rarely result in a net positive outcome. Counter-Strike 2 lacks in its multiplayer experience, as anti-cheat has not yet been added to the game. Expect to be queued with cheaters/hackers every third game or less. However, Valve, specifically cs2 developers are working on an anti-cheat.

Audio / Visual: Counter-Strike 2 significantly upgrades its visual fidelity compared to its predecessor. The textures are sharper, environments more detailed, and lighting effects more dynamic, creating a more immersive battlefield. Character models and weapon designs are more intricate, enhancing the overall aesthetic appeal. However, some minor graphical glitches and occasional frame drops do occur. The sound design in Counter-Strike 2 is top-notch, with realistic gunfire, footsteps, and environmental noises that enhance situational awareness and immersion. The updated audio engine provides clearer, more precise directional sound cues, crucial for competitive play. However, some players have reported inconsistencies in sound propagation and occasional audio bugs, which can detract from the experience.

Overall: Counter-Strike 2 may not be perfect right now, but there is hope for the future of the game with less cheaters.

Rating:       9/10

Counter strike 2 was severely mishandled. 

New smokes are a solution to a problem no one really complained about. One can argue that one-ways were just utilization of, well, utility to it's fullest. You can't really complain about one-ways being unfair because the very purpose of a utility grenade is to create unfair situation, in a same way you wouldn't complain about being blinded from a flash bang.

Subtick system is extremely buggy with peekers advantage being problem now more than ever. It's also borderline false advertising calling it a tick independent gameplay because actions are still handled per tick, sub tick system just puts time stamps on them so they can be processed in a right order, like rewinding time. What you see is NOT what you get.

Lastly we are left with a graphics improvements of maps. The fact that graphics improvements were such a big deal in valves advertising demonstrates a severe disconnect from their player base, because anyone loosely familiar with Counter Strike knows that everyone kills their graphics with various scripts to max the fps and don't care about graphics.

Wrapping things up with missing content from previous game (Actual content, not colored pixels), basically unfunctioning anti-cheat, and a mess that is new premiere ranking. It's sad to see such a well renowned franchise such a disgraceful manner, as well as laziness and disconnect from Valve unlike anything seen before.

The number 2, the second iteration of Counter Strike, should have been something great and done with care and effort. Instead, it was subpar and underwhelming.

Counter Strike deserved better, as well as the player base.

This sole question, this "Do you recommend this game?" seems more like an anachronism in most cases, especially when it comes to the [i]Counter-Strike[/i] phenomenon; to be specific, the most recent and trendy one. This is noteworthy because the outdated versions are almost always replete with players as well as the newest one.

For me, [i]C.S.: G.O.[/i] was the purest form of escapism in the dark days of COVID-19, and then a hiatus of 2-3 years and a return to this polished, glossier version called [i]C.S. 2[/i]. But have I ever enjoyed it, as I have enjoyed other groundbreaking (or better said, heartbreaking) titles? Or is this a mere vessel for my friends and I to gather around, point at colorful pixels, and chat our dilemmas, problems, issues, and fond moments out? Does [i]C.S.[/i] have inherent qualities that make it irreplaceable or it was just an unspoken consensus that brought us to the lobby of this game at the height of the pandemic? These are the questions - and here comes the punchline - that I think about whenever the crazy matchmaking algorithm sets me up against an obvious cheater or someone way above my league (and to any casual player like me, both are the same in effect).

There are no glaring issues, and if only the matchmaking (along with the anti-cheat system) worked better, then [i]C.S.[/i] would've been untouchable and among the stars.

text:
First Impressions
CS
, now also known as CS2, has been a staple in the gaming world for years. I’ve sunk countless hours into this game, and it’s still as thrilling as the first time I played it. If you’re into first-person shooters, this game is a must-try. It’s got everything you’d want: intense gameplay, strategic depth, and a massive community.

Gameplay
The gameplay is where CS
truly shines. You’re either a terrorist or a counter-terrorist, and your objective changes based on the map and mode. Whether it’s planting or defusing bombs or rescuing hostages, every round is packed with adrenaline. The game demands quick reflexes and smart tactics. One wrong move, and you’re done for. It’s this high-stakes environment that keeps you on the edge of your seat.

Graphics and Sound
Even though CS
runs on the older Source Engine, the graphics hold up pretty well. The maps are detailed and have a distinct aesthetic, and the recent updates have only made them better. The sound design is top-notch too. From the crack of a sniper rifle to the footsteps of an enemy creeping up behind you, the audio cues are crucial and add a layer of immersion.

The Community and Competitive Scene
One of the best things about CS
is its community. Millions of players from around the world jump into the game daily, ensuring you always have someone to play with. The competitive scene is massive. Watching pro players in tournaments is just as fun as playing, if not more so. The ranking system is also well-designed, pitting you against players of similar skill levels, which keeps the matches challenging and fair.

What I Love
Addictive Gameplay: The fast-paced, tactical gameplay never gets old. Each match feels like a fresh challenge.
Active Community: There’s always someone online, and the community is passionate about the game.
Frequent Updates: Valve keeps the game fresh with regular updates, new skins, and maps.
What Could Be Better
Steep Learning Curve: It’s not the most newbie-friendly game. Be prepared to die a lot when you first start.
Cheaters: Despite Valve’s efforts, cheating can still be an issue. It’s frustrating when you encounter a hacker.
Outdated Engine: The Source Engine is showing its age. While the game looks good, it doesn’t compare to newer titles in terms of graphics.
Final Thoughts
CS
, or CS2 if you prefer, is a legendary game in the FPS genre. Despite some minor issues, it’s incredibly fun and rewarding. Whether you’re looking to casually play with friends or climb the competitive ranks, this game has something for everyone. If you haven’t tried it yet, you’re missing out on one of the best gaming experiences out there.

In summary, Counter-Strike remains a phenomenal game that offers thrilling and strategic gameplay. text: CS 1 personally was better in my opinion in terms of its overall enjoyment and options available. To elaborate, the game even when it was not free I felt offered more to the user for their buck so to speak (time), then what is offered currently in CS2. Despite the hacker issues CSGO has always had, the introduction of prime did have some hackers stray away, however this without a new anti cheat could not be helped. The game offered a fun (all be it flawed) ranking system, that was very challenging, even borderline rage inducing at time, but that is what made it challenging and different from other competitive shooters. Making every rank up, and the road to it, so fulfilling and enjoyable. Especially when you found a good team to play with. In fact many of my friends I game with to this day I met in a random csgo competitive match. Many players took competitive fairly seriously, and so communication was key, and was often times had in matches, however in CS2 this is not the case, and I'd say the introduction of premier and map specific ranks vs 1 total rank overall, has drastically brought down the player base that it once had and the enjoyment competitive brought. With that most people do not care about their rank or if they lose or win a match, because a point system means each match you will go up or down, but there is no title associated with it, and there is no fun in guessing if you'll get that next rank up or not or de rank. Meaning you always had to play your best because you never knew the outcome. Additionally, because each map has it's own rank most people don't care if they lose a match, because they have several ranks on various ones, and it doesn't really matter. It took away the fun or putting a Q of all the maps and learning them cohesively for your overall rank, vs just one map for 1 rank. With all this in mind, most players iv'e encoutered in all my play time thus far on CS2 do not talk and do not care about the match, making it less enjoyable. And when maps are cared about, and you win, I never feel satisfied or get that wow moment, or the fun I once did, because I see my rank and then I see multiple other ranks, that are lower or higher, not motivating me to push further for my rank, as I now want to get them all to the same level making me care less. The point system in premier is the same way, I know how much I will lose or win, an in any event, it is not the same as a rank, and so when in a game and I see a player with 20k points vs 14k I do not get the same distinction or awe I use to when I would see lets say a MG 2 and a LE in the same game. Moving forward, in CSGO 1 there was a vast amount of public servers always populated, and events going on at certain times that the whole community was invested in, even live matches between teams broad cast from the mane menu people would watch. However in comparison, CS2 feels lacking. Overall the graphics are better, and the game feels fairly good, but CS has never been a game most players play for beauty. With that, I think it is a great game with great promise, however lacks the main component it once had pushing it to be a competitive, fun shooter for those to grind out and improve to go up the ranks, I think with the implementation of a ranking system similar to that of the old CSGO, it could have great promise!

Counter-Strike 2 brings the franchise into the next generation with an exhilarating mix of tactical gameplay, refined mechanics, and stunning visuals. One of the standout features of CS2 is the enhanced gunplay. The weapons feel as satisfying as ever, with a more refined recoil system that rewards skill and practice. However, there is a downside worth mentioning: the anti-cheat system. It can sometimes disrupt the experience, especially for those who are simply enjoying the game without engaging in any illicit activity. While updates to the anti-cheat system are expected, it’s something to be aware of in the meantime.

Despite the anti-cheat hiccups, CS2 delivers an exceptional experience overall. The gameplay is more thrilling and polished than ever before, and the community-driven aspect of the game continues to thrive. If you're a fan of tactical shooters, CS2 is a must-play, and the anti-cheat issues, while noticeable, are unlikely to take away from the overall enjoyment once they’re resolved. Highly recommended for both veterans and newcomers!

text:
Counter-Strike 2 is undeniably one of the most thrilling multiplayer experiences out there. The intensity of matches, the satisfaction of a well-executed strategy, and the joy of teaming up with friends make it a game that keeps pulling you back in. Add to that the incredible skin ecosystem, where every weapon feels like an extension of your personality, and it’s easy to see why CS2 continues to capture the hearts of players worldwide. The trading and collecting aspects add depth to the game, giving players something to chase beyond just wins.

But as much as I enjoy the game, it’s impossible to ignore its glaring flaws. The community market is a disaster—not just frustrating to navigate but also absurdly expensive. With Valve taking up to 15% commission on every transaction, it feels like players are being gouged for simply participating in the economy. The lack of advanced search options, classification tools, and the constant duplication of listings when scrolling make the experience infuriating for anyone trying to find or trade skins.

And then there’s the cheater problem, which has completely undermined the competitive integrity of the game. It’s been over a year since CS2 launched, and the anti-cheat system still feels like it doesn’t exist. Match after match, I’ve had to deal with cheaters—some blatantly obvious, others trying to hide it by playing just well enough to avoid detection. What’s worse, my achievement medal won’t even reflect my honest efforts because I’m constantly up against these unfair players. It’s incredibly disheartening to know my performance—and likely my rating—will be dragged down simply because Valve can’t or won’t fix the problem.

Kicking cheaters is nearly impossible, too. The voting system is broken when cheaters queue together, making it impossible to kick them as a group. And even when they’re not grouped up, players are often reluctant to kick a cheater on their own team because it gives them an advantage. I’ve only managed to kick a cheater once, which speaks volumes about how poorly designed this system is.

There’s also the issue of brand-new accounts being matched against long-time players. It’s painfully obvious when a brand-new account is being used to cheat, yet there’s no penalty system or separation to stop this from happening. How is it fair that older, more established accounts are forced to deal with these throwaway accounts in every match?

Counter-Strike 2 could easily be the definitive competitive FPS, but these glaring issues—the lack of a proper anti-cheat system, the broken vote-kick mechanics, the mismatch of new accounts with veterans, and the overpriced, frustrating community market—are holding it back. Valve, we love this game, but it’s time to step up and make it fair for the honest players who’ve stuck with you through the years.

text:
While Counter-Strike has been a staple of the FPS genre for decades at this point, never has its issues been more apparent.
The pandemic of software exploiters destroying valves own matchmaking system has never been worse, and that is not new nor about to change. Cheaters being caught doing their thing on external services to a lesser yet still non-significant extent is also a thing and has been for a solid 20 years.

It gets to the point where you never know if you're playing vs another player who has access to the same information, relies on his or her own physical input to perform in the game. Which either drives you away from the game entirely, makes you question your own skill/decision making/sanity or makes those of a more malleable and weaker moral constitution indulge in the same behavior.

If steps are not taken towards cracking down on the cheating issues on a larger than bi-personal scale things will not change. Without a form of real-id-gaming-tag i have no faith in seeing repeat offenders be deterred from returning again and again each time with a new account. The only repercussion felt is the loss of a throwaway account.

It hurts, it really does to see a game that i love and have spent thousands of hours playing, learning, practicing and spectating/viewing tournaments and demos be in this situation. When the casting crew on competitive-world level tournaments make jokes about the amount of cheaters on public servers.. its bad..
